entries.title: Zechariah 1:1 "In the eighth month of the second year"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:1 "In the eighth month of the second year" This refers to October or November of either 520 or 519 B.C., depending on whether one uses the Syrian or Babylonian calendar. The Jews had been back in Palestine for eighteen years at this point. The temple rebuilding, which had begun under Sheshbazzar (Ezra 5:16), had not been finished under Zerubbabel.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE CALENDARS

▣ "Darius" This refers to Darius I, son of Hystapes, also called "the great." He reigned from 522 to 486 B.C. over the Persian Empire; therefore, his second year would be 520 B.C. He was the successor of Cyrus II's son, Cambyses II (530-522 B.C.), who committed suicide because of Egyptian military victories. Darius was not part of the royal line, but he married a royal daughter in order to legitimize his reign. He searched the Persian records and when he discovered the Edict of Cyrus II (cf. Ezra 5-6) he rejected the legal case of the Samaritans and even helped provide money for the rebuilding of the temple.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF PERSIA

▣ "the word of the Lord came" God's mercy and patience is demonstrated by the fact that as He sent His word in the past, and it was originally rejected (cf. Zech. 1:6), He now sends it again. God wants a personal, ethical, obedient relationship with people of faith!

This introductory prophetic phrase is characteristic of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, but not in this exact form in Isaiah.

These visions (Zech.1:7-6:15) were not exclusively from the imagination of Zechariah, but were from YHWH. The genre questions have always been:

  1. Did YHWH communicate His message in apocalyptic visions?
  2. Did Zechariah structure YHWH's message in a series of visions?

These same questions relate to poetry, fables, parables, and textual design. Is the Bible dictated by the Spirit or does the human author participate? The variety of Scriptural genres and structures implies a creative element on the part of the human author.

  1. Joyce G. Baldwin, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, p. 74, says, "One of the important contributions of modern scholarship to our understanding of the Bible is the realization that its truth is expressed in literary forms and structures as well as in words."
  2. R. K. Harrison, Introduction to the Old Testament, p. 950, says, "probably the only legitimate question that can be raised in this regard, however, is whether the visions were real experiences or merely a literary form, as in later apocalyptic writings."
  3. These forms and structures were contemporary with the inspired authors, not radically new or different (see Hinckley G. Mitchell, ICC, p. 117).

This does not affect the complete inspiration of the Bible, but does reveal how God cooperates with His human creatures. Our "in His image" (i.e., Gen. 1:26-27) is an awesome, mysterious, and pervasive concept (i.e., Ps. 8:4-8)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BIBLE (its uniqueness and inspiration)

▣ "Zechariah" The name means "YHWH remembers" (BDB 272). This is a very common Hebrew name, which is used twenty-nine times in the OT. Its meaning seems especially significant in light of the returning exiles' view that God had reestablished His covenant with them. He was a contemporary of Haggai. When one compares the dates (i.e., Hag. 1:1 with Zech. 1:1) Zechariah began preaching about two months later than Haggai.

SPECIAL TOPIC: POST EXILIC CHART

▣ "the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo saying" When one compares Ezra 5:1; 6:14 with Zech. 1:1,7, he sees that the father of Zechariah is omitted. There have been several theories about the omission:

  1. Hebrew genealogies often skip generations
  2. the early church fathers said that this refers, not to physical lineage, but to spiritual lineage (i.e., Jerome), Iddo being a tribal family group of Levites who returned to Jerusalem (cf. Neh. 12:4,16)
  3. others say that for some reason Berechiah did not live up to his priestly lineage
  4. Zechariah's father had died and he was raised by his grandfather, Iddo
  5. it refers to the faithful witness mentioned in Isa. 8:2 whose father was Je-berechiah ("YHWH" blesses)

It is obvious that Zechariah was a prophet and a priest (cf. Jer. 1:1; Ezek. 1:1).

entries.title: Zechariah Introduction
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
INTRODUCTION TO ZECHARIAH

  1. UNIQUENESS

    1. This book is pivotal in our understanding of both apocalyptic literature and eschatology.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

    2. Surprisingly Zechariah 1-8 are alluded to extensively in the book of the Revelation, while Zechariah 9-14 are alluded to often in the Gospels.
      1. Zechariah is seen by NT authors to refer to Jesus (direct quote)
        1. Matt. 21:5; John 12:15 ‒ Zech. 9:9
        2. Matt. 27:9-10 ‒ Zech. 11:12-13
        3. John 19:32 ‒ Zech. 12:10
        4. Matt. 26:31; Mark 14:27 ‒ Zech. 13:7
      2. allusions to Zechariah 1-8 in Revelation
        1. Zech. 1:8 ‒ Rev. 6:2,4; 19:11
        2. Zech. 2:1-2 ‒ Rev. 11:1
        3. Zech. 2:10 ‒ Rev. 21:3
        4. Zech. 3:1 ‒ Rev. 12:10
        5. Zech. 4:3 ‒ Rev. 11:4
        6. Zech. 4:10-14 ‒ Rev. 5:6
        7. Zech. 6:2 ‒ Rev. 6:4,5
        8. Zech. 6:3 ‒ Rev. 6:2; 19:11
        9. Zech. 6:5 ‒ Rev. 7:1
        10. Zech. 6:6 ‒ Rev. 6:2,5; 19:11
      3. allusions to Zechariah 9-14 in the Gospels
        1. Zech. 9:2-4 ‒ Matt. 11:21-22; Luke 10:13-14
        2. Zech. 9:11 ‒ Matt. 26:28; Mark 14:24; Luke 22:20
        3. Zech. 11:12 ‒ Matt. 26:15
        4. Zech. 12:10 ‒ Matt. 24:30
        5. Zech. 13:7 ‒ Matt. 26:31; Mark 14

    3. Zechariah quotes extensively from the major eighth century prophets
      1. in the North, Amos and Hosea
      2. in the South, Isaiah and Micah
      3. as well as the seventh century prophets, Jeremiah and Ezekiel
        He brings their insights to bear on his day and the last days. This shows that the prophets of Israel and Judah had access to each other's books.
        SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)
        SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW CANON
        SPECIAL TOPIC: POST EXILIC CHART

    4. This book is a good example of apocalyptic language. This is a literary genre which tries to document future events by means of figurative, imaginative imagery. It was often used by Jewish authors in tension-filled times to express the hope of God's people that He was/is in control. Three good books that have helped me are
      1. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Langauge of Prophecy and Apocalyptic
      2. Sandy and Giese, Cracking OT Codes
      3. Fee and Stuart, How To Read the Bible For All Its Worth
      4. C. B. Caird, The Langauge and Imagery of the Bible

    5. This book is also very Messianic. He is God's agent of permanent change in human history. Zechariah, like Isaiah (cf. Isa. 52:13-53:12), reveals a suffering Messiah (cf. Gen. 3:15), which was so unexpected by the rabbis.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIAH
      SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIANIC ERA
      SPECIAL TOPIC: A SUFFERING MESSIAH

    6. Jerome, the translator of the Latin Vulgate, called Zechariah the most obscure book in the Old Testament. This shows the level of shocking imagery that Zechariah used to reveal God's message.

  2. AUTHOR

    1. Zechariah means "YHWH remembers" or "One remembered by YHWH" (BDB 272). This prophet's name gives hope to the exiled Jews who wondered if their Covenant God remembered them. Haggai and Zechariah's call to rebuild the temple is physical evidence that the Abrahamic, Mosaic, and Davidic covenant promises are restored to the post-exilic community.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: TABERNACLE OF THE WILDERNESS
      SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S COVENANT REQUIREMENTS OF ISRAEL
      SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

    2. Zechariah was a very common Hebrew name. It was spelled two ways in the English Bibles: Zechariah or Zachariah because of the Hebrew name's translation into Greek. There are twenty-seven people in the English OT who spell it with an "e" and two who spell it with an "a."

    3. Zechariah 1:1 tells us that he was a priest (cf. Ezra 5:1; 6:14; Neh. 12:4,16). Why his ancestor, Berechiah, is omitted from the list is uncertain. This would make him a post-exilic prophet, like Haggai, Malachi, and possibly Obadiah and Joel.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: LEVITICAL PRIESTS
      SPECIAL TOPIC: POST EXILIC CHART

    4. Many modern scholars deny the unity of the book of Zechariah. This is because
      1. chapters 1-8 are so different from chapters 9-14. In chapters 1-8 the prophet is named and dates are given. The setting is obviously post-exilic. This section is alluded to extensively by John in his book of the Revelation.
      2. However, Zechariah 9-14 are undated. There is no prophet named. There is no obvious historical setting. This section is alluded to most often in the Gospels. However, this literary structure is common in several OT prophets (e.g., Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel).
          In Matt. 27:9 Jesus attributes a quote to Jeremiah which is from Zech. 11:12-13 (see full exegetical note at Matt. 27:9). This was the beginning of the trend toward denying authorship of chapters 9-14 to Zechariah.
        SPECIAL TOPIC: MATTHEW 27:9
      3. However, even the Dead Sea Scrolls have Zechariah as a unity.
          There are several internal grammatical and lexical items which point to a unity.
        1. the use of the number "two" (Zech. 4:3; 5:9; 6:1; 11:7; 13:8)
        2. the use of a VOCATIVE (Zech. 2:7,10; 3:2,8; 4:7; 9:9,13; 11:1-2; 13:7)
        3. the use of the phrase, "go to and fro," which is unique to Zechariah (Zech. 7:14; 9:8)
        4. the repeated use of "saith the Lord" (used sixteen times)
        5. the Qal form of "to dwell" or "to inhabit" ( BDB 442, Zech. 2:8; 7:7; 12:6; 14:10)
          (These are taken from R. K. Harrison's Introduction to the Old Testament, p. 954). For further discussion of the unity of the book see E. J. Young's Introduction to the Old Testament, p. 280).

  3. DATE

    1. From Zech. 1:1 we learn that the prophet began his ministry in the second year of Darius. Most scholars assert that this is Darius I Hystaspes (522-486 B.C.), who took over the kingdom after Cambyses II (530-522 B.C.), Cyrus II’s son, committed suicide.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF PERSIA

    2. This would make the date 520-519 B.C. He preached about two years (cf. Zech. 1:7; 7:1).

    3. Haggai and Zechariah are dated more precisely than any other OT books.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: HAGGAI

  4. PURPOSE

    1. The major purpose of the book is to encourage the returning Jews to rebuild the temple (cf. Ezra 5). This was started by Sheshbazzar (cf. Ezra 1:8; 5:16), but had not been continued under Zerubbabel (cf. Ezra 2:1-2). The temple had been neglected for eighteen years. Haggai asserts that this is because of the apathy of the people (cf. Hag. 1:1-11), while Ezra implies that it was the political maneuvers of the surrounding provinces, especially Samaria.

    2. Both Haggai and Zechariah address the issue of rebuilding the temple (cf. Zechariah 1-8), but Zechariah also covers many more issues (cf. Zechariah 9-14).

    3. I must admit I struggle with prophetic and apocalyptic language. Its imagery is hard to put into a specific historical setting. Exegesis of the texts often does not reveal the meaning. I love God's word and do not want to add to it or take away from it (cf. Deut. 4:2; 12:32; Prov. 30:5-6; Matt. 5:17-19). Here are some resouces that have helped me in this dilemma.
      1. A Guide to Biblical Prophecy by Carl E. Amending and W. Ward Basque
      2. How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth by Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, chapter 10
      3. My Servants the Prophets by Edward J. Young
      4. Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic by D. Brent Sandy
      5. New International Dictionary of Old Testament Theology and Exegesis, vol. 4, pp. 1067-1078
      6. The Langauge and Imagery of the Bible by G. B. Caird
      7. YouTube lectures by Steve Gregg (thenarrowpath.com) who is a partial preterist

  5. BRIEF SAMPLE OUTLINE (taken from Introduction to the Old Testament, by R. K. Harrison, p. 950)

    1. Dated prophecies, Zechariah 1-8
      1. Introduction and call to repentance, Zech. 1:1-6
      2. Eight visions, Zech. 1:7-6:8
        1. four horsemen; the promise of divine restoration, Zech. 1:7-17
        2. four destroying horns and four smiths, Zech. 1:18-21 (Heb. 2:1-4)
        3. the immeasurable greatness of Jerusalem, Zech. 2:1-13 (Heb. 2:5-17)
        4. the cleansing of Joshua; an oracle to him, Zech. 3:1-10
        5. the seven-branched lampstand, Zech. 4:1-14
        6. the large, flying scroll, Zech. 5:1-4
        7. the woman in an ephah removed to Babylon, Zech. 5:5-11
        8. four horse-drawn chariots traversing the earth, Zech. 6:1-8
      3. Historical section: Joshua symbolic of the Messiah, Zech. 6:9-15 (I think this is a ninth vision)
      4. An inquiry of Zechariah concerning fasting, Zech. 7:1-8:23

    2. Undated prophecies, Zechariah 9-14
      1. Judgment of national enemies; the coming of the peaceful prince, Zech. 9:1-17
      2. Gathering in of the chosen flock by the divine leader, Zech. 10:1-12
      3. Good and foolish shepherds; the suffering of the flock, Zech. 11:1-17
      4. Eschatological oracles, Zech. 12:1-13:6
      5. The purifying judgment of Israel and the blessings of the divine kingdom, Zech. 13:7-14:21

  6. THE MEANING OF THE EIGHT VISIONS

    1. The angels on colored horses (cf. Zech. 1:7-17) — God knows what is happening on earth, especially as it relates to His plan of universal redemption through a Jewish Messiah. The Jews must be reestablished in Jerusalem for God's plan to manifest in history (i.e., Dan. 9:24-27).
      SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

    2. The four horns and the four craftsmen (cf. Zech. 1:18-21) — God allowed pagan nations to judge His idolatrous people (cf. Zech. 1:15), but now He will judge them for their excess and pride. World empires are directed by God for His redemptive purposes.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #2
      SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SECOND COMING, IV.

    3. The measuring of Jerusalem (cf. Zech. 2:1-13) — God will restore His people to the Promised Land and renew and expand the covenant. YHWH Himself will be with them and protect them as in the Exodus experience. But remember, most covenants and promises are conditional of covenant obedience and loyalty!
      SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT
      SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

    4. Joshua forgiven and restored (cf. Zech. 3:1-10) — Joshua as High Priest stands for the Jewish nation. He is forgiven and restored, which shows in very clear symbols that the sacrificial system and, thereby, the covenant is fully restored and functioning. The Messianic element shows the priestly aspect of the Messiah’s work (cf. Psalm110; Isaiah 53; Heb. 1:3; 5:6,10; 6:20; 7:17; 8:1; 10:12; 12:2).
      SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS AS HIGH PRIEST
      SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SUPERIORITY OF THE NEW COVENANT OVER THE MOSAIC COVENANT

    5. The lampstand (cf. Zech. 4:1-14) — God’s power, not human power, will reestablish the covenant (i.e., rebuilt temple as a symbol/sign). God will use Spirit-empowered human instrumentality (i.e., Joshua and Zerubbabel).
      SPECIAL TOPIC: LAMPSTAND

    6. The flying scroll (cf. Zech. 5:1-4) — Symbol of God’s judgment on covenant breaking Jews among His people, which will result in the destruction of the violators.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT REQUIREMENTS OF ISRAEL

    7. Wickedness in a basket (cf. Zech. 5:5-11) — Rebellion (idolatry) against God will be caged in a basket and removed to the place of human arrogance and idolatry (i.e., Shinar = Babylon).
      SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

    8. The four chariots pulled by colored horses (cf. Zech. 6:1-8) — This is parallel to the first vision. God is present and sovereign in all the world (i.e., Dan. 2:21; Romans 9).

  7. Please read the quotes from D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks, found in Contextual Insights to Daniel 11, F. These insights into the nature of apocalyptic literature will be very helpful as we study and attempt to interpret the book of Zechariah.

*Although they are not inspired, paragraph divisions are the key to understanding and following the original author's intent. Each modern translation has divided and summarized the paragraphs. Every paragraph has one central topic, truth, or thought. Each version encapsulates that topic in its own distinct way. As you read the text, ask yourself which translation fits your understanding of the subject and verse divisions.

In every chapter we must read the Bible first and try to identify its subjects (paragraphs), then compare our understanding with the modern versions. Only when we understand the original author's intent by following his logic and presentation can we truly understand the Bible. Only the original author is inspired—readers have no right to change or modify the message. Bible readers do have the responsibility of applying the inspired truth to their day and their lives.

Note that all technical terms and abbreviations are explained fully in the following Special Topics: Hebrew Grammatical Terms and Glossary.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. The first six verses are an introduction to the whole book. They emphasize the requirement of a covenant relationship (faith and obedience) and specify the need for ongoing repentance.

    God's word is sure and permanent (cf. Isa. 45:23, 55:11; Matt. 5:17-20). How each generation of believers responds to Him (personal) and it (doctrinal and lifestyle) determines their blessing or cursing (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 27-29).

    SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS (OT)

    SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

    SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

    SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

  2. Beginning in Zech. 1:7 and continuing through Zech. 6:15 is a series of eight visions and their interpretations (angelic mediators). There are apocalyptic elements in these visions.
    1. angelic actors and interpreters
    2. colors
    3. animals
    4. numbers

      SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

  3. There seems to be a similar opening (Zech.1:7-17) and closing (Zech. 6:1-5).
    1. four colored horses patrol the earth at YHWH's behest
    2. four chariots of colored horses patrol the earth at YHWH's behest

      The apocalyptic themes of God's knowledge and sovereignty control and interpret history (i.e., Dan. 2:21). All eight visions must be taken together as one emphasis and related to chapters 9-14. See D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, pp. 47-50.

  4. Much modern scholarship is recognizing a particular type of two-way stair step parallelism called chiasmus in both Zech. 1:7-6:15 and 9-14 (cf. Joyce Baldwin, Tyndale OT Commentary, "Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi," pp. 74-81). If this is true, then the fourth and fifth visions take an emphasized structural position.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Zechariah 1:2 "The Lord was very angry with your fathers"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:2 "The Lord was very angry with your fathers" The word "anger" (BDB 893) appears twice in Zech. 1:2 and has an intensified connotation, "was very angry" (cf. Zech. 1:14-15). This is an anthropomorphic phrase putting human emotions on God, and yet, human vocabulary is the only means we have to understand and communicate thoughts about God.
SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

For the term "Lord" (YHWH) see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

The expression "very angry" (BDB 893) is used several times in Zechariah (cf. Zech. 1:2 [twice]; 1:15 [twice]; 7:12; and 8:14). YHWH was angry

  1. with His people because of their sin (cf. Zech. 7:12; 8:14)
  2. also at the nations He used to judge His people (cf. Zech. 1:15)

The phrase "your fathers" refers primarily to the previous history of Jewish rebellion (cf. Zech. 1:4) and, by implication, to Haggai and Zechariah's generation, who had been neglectful in rebuilding the temple.

This opening paragraph has several levels of direct quotes. It is hard to identify the ANTECEDENTS of the PRONOUNS. The term "them" of Zech. 1:3 and the "they" and "us" of v. 6, refer to the current generation of Jews living in Jerusalem and the surrounding area (cf. Zech. 1:3-6).

entries.title: Zechariah 1:3 "says the Lord of hosts"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:3 "says the Lord of hosts" This is a direct quote from God (cf. Isa. 31:6; Mal 3:7). This phrase is found in the Hebrew text three times in Zech. 1:3, once in 1:4, and again in 1:6 (also note Zech. 1:12 and 16). The title "Lord of hosts" occurs at least fifty times in Zechariah.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

▣ "Return" This is the Hebrew word shub (BDB 996, KB 1427) in a Qal IMPERATIVE form (as in Zech. 1:4). Zechariah 1:3 and 6 are the key to this opening paragraph. It signified a turning from idols and returning to YHWH (cf. Isa. 31:6-7). It is used extensively by Jeremiah for spiritual conversion (e.g., Jer. 15:19; 18:8,11). God always takes the initiative in human repentance (cf. Jer. 31:18; Lam. 5:21; Prov. 8:3,7,19; John 6:44,65; Acts 5:31; 8:22; 2 Tim. 2:25). However, God has structured His Covenant in such a way that humans must respond in repentance and faith to Him, both initially and throughout life (cf. Mark 1:15; Acts 2:38,41; 3:16,19; 20:21). Because these were already covenant people it is uncertain whether this text is referring to

  1. initial personal salvation (cf. Isa. 55:6-7)
  2. what we would call today a rededication experience (cf. Zech. 1:4,6; Rev. 2:5,16,21,22; 3:3,19,20)

In the OT descendants of Abraham were part of the people of God, but it is obvious from the OT itself that all of them did not have a personal faith relationship with God that impacted their daily lives. Religion, ritual, and self-righteous legalism are always barriers and blinders.

It is theologically significant that Zechariah calls for a repentant response on the part of the people of God. The visions of Zech. 1:8-6:15 then proclaim God's sovereign acts on behalf of His people. Notice the balance―God's sovereign initiative demands a human response.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: PREDESTINATION (Calvinism) VERSES HUMAN FREE WILL (Arminianism)

▣ "to Me" Notice the personal element (cf. Isa. 44:22, very similar to John's Gospel). It is God who we need more than any of His gifts. Covenant faith is personal! Truth is personal (cf. John 8:32; 14:6).

I have enjoyed and benefitted from Joyce D. Baldwin's Tyndale Commentaries on both Daniel and the post-exilic prophets (Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi). Here is an example of her insight.

"The new generation was free to make a new start (Ezek. 18:14ff); the Lord would return to them, despite the covenant-breaking of past generations if they would return to Him" Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi (p. 87).

The invitation of Ezekiel 18 (both individual and corporate) is still open (as is the seventh day rest of Heb. 3; 4)! This chapter is new OT imagery for the "seventh day of rest" (cf. Psalm 95; Hebrews 3-4).

▣ "that I may return to you" Repentance restores fellowship with God (cf. Mal. 3:7; James 4:8; 1 John 1:9; the negative form in 2 Chr. 15:2). The term shub (BDB 996, KB 1427) is used twice in Zech. 1:3; once in 1:4; and once in 1:6.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPEPTANCE (OT)

entries.title: Zechariah 1:4 "the former prophets"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:4 "the former prophets" This phrase becomes a technical term in later rabbinical writings for the "historical books" of Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings. Here it refers to the pre-exilic writing prophets of the eighth and seventh centuries (cf. Zech. 7:7; 2 Chr. 24:19; 36:15).

▣ "Return now from your evil ways and from your evil deeds" This is an allusion from previous prophets (e.g., Isa. 1:16-19; Jer. 18:11; 25:5; 35:15; Ezek. 33:11). God's people rejected both God and His covenant requirements and went after other gods (i.e., fertility worship). This was the spiritual cause of the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles. These post-exilic inhabitants of Jerusalem must be different!

The phrases "your evil ways" and "your evil deeds" function as a hendiadys. The term "ways" is used as imagery for lifestyle. Biblical faith (see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL) is

  1. personal
  2. creedal
  3. lifestyle

This lifestyle obedience is expressed early in Gen. 18:19 (cf. Jdgs. 2:22; Ps. 119:1). The related imagery is "walk" (e.g., Prov. 6:20-22; Jer. 7:24; 10:9; Eph. 14:1,17; 5:2,15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT REQUIREMENTS OF ISRAEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

▣ "But they did not listen or give heed to Me" The two negated VERBS "listen" (BDB 1033, KB 1570) and "give heed" (BDB 904, KB 1151) reflect Deut. 6:4, which denotes hearing and obeying (cf. Deut. 5:32-33; 6:1-3). It is not enough to know God's words, they must be lived out (cf. James 1:22-25)!

The phrase "give heed" is from the Hebrew root which means "pay close attention to" (cf. Jer. 6:17; 11:7,8). This phrase is an allusion to Jer. 7:24,26; 17:23; 19:15; 29:19.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEMA

entries.title: Zechariah 1:5 "Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:5 "Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever" This verse emphasizes the frailty of humanity (both evil and good) versus the eternality of God (cf. Ps. 103:15-18; Mal. 3:6) and His word (cf. Isa. 40:8; 45:23; 55:11; 59:21; Matt. 5:17-18; 24:35).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

entries.title: Zechariah 1:6 "My words and My statutes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:6 "My words and My statutes" God's revealed truths and covenant requirements are called by many terms, as Ps. 19:7-9 clearly shows.

  1. "the law of the Lord," Zech. 1:7
  2. "the testimony of the Lord," Zech. 1:7
  3. "the precepts of the Lord," Zech. 1:8
  4. "the commandment of the Lord," Zech. 1:8
  5. "the fear of the Lord," Zech. 1:9
  6. "the judgments of the Lord," Zech. 1:9

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION

▣ "My servants the prophets" Initially the Patriarchs are designated "servants" (e.g., Gen. 18:5). However, it came to refer to the family of Abraham collectively (i.e., Jacob, Israel, cf. Isa. 41:8,9; 42:1,19; 43:10; 44:1,2); then specifically to David the king of united Israel (e.g., 2 Sam. 7:5,8,19,20; Isa. 37:35). The phrase is used often in 2 Kings (cf. 2 Kgs. 9:7; 17:13,23; 21:10; 24:2) for God's speakers, the prophets. The phrase is also used extensively of the prophets in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 7:25; 25:4; 26:5; 29:19; 35:15). It is obvious from the number of allusions in this context that Zechariah knew Jeremiah's writings well.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MY SERVANT

▣ "overtake your fathers" This is hunting imagery (BDB 673, KB 727, Hiphil PERFECT, cf. Exod. 14:9; 15:9; Deut. 19:6) and it seems to refer to "the cursings" of Lev. 26 and Deut. 28 if the covenant was violated.

▣"they repented"  See SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT).

▣ "to do to us in accordance with our ways and our deeds" This may be an allusion to Lam. 2:17. Each generation must respond to the covenant. The danger of religion is that it can become a family tradition instead of a personal faith. "The fathers" repented, but only after God's judgment!

For "our deeds" see full notes at Gal. 6:7.

entries.title: Zechariah 1:7 "On the twenty-fourth day"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:7 "On the twenty-fourth day" It is uncertain why the twenty-fourth day was so significant, but it is referred to extensively by the prophet Haggai (cf. Hag. 1:15; 2:10,18,20). This exact date seems to be February 15, 519 B.C.

The post-exilic prophets Haggai and Zechariah are mentioned together in Ezra 5:1 and 6:14.

Post-Exilic Chart

▣ "the eleventh month" This would be February-March, three months from the date in Zech. 1:1. Zechariah 1:7 begins a series of eight visions which continue through Zech. 6:15.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE CALENDARS

▣ "Shebat" The name of this month is a post-exilic Babylonian loan word (BDB 987) which means "to kill," "to strike," or "to destroy." BDB suggests it refers to the rainy season which included floods and storms. It occurs only here in the OT. Other Babylonian dates (cf. Zech. 7:1) appear in Ezra-Nehemiah, which is the same historical period (i.e., early post-exilic or the Persian period).

For a good discussion of the calendars in use in the Ancient Near East, see

  1. Jack Finegan, Light From the Ancient Past: the Archeological Background of the Hebrew-Christian Religion, vol. 2, pp. 552-598
  2. Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 1, pp. 178-194

entries.title: Zechariah 1:8 "I saw"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:8 "I saw" In Zechariah the Hebrew word "see" (BDB 906, KB 1157) is often used to introduce a new vision.

  1. "I saw," Zech. 1:8
  2. "I will show you," Zech. 1:9
  3. "I lifted my eyes and looked," Zech. 1:18
  4. "the Lord showed me," Zech. 1:20
  5. "I lifted up my eyes and looked," Zech. 2:1
  6. "he showed me," Zech. 3:1
  7. "what do you see?" "I see," Zech. 4:2
  8. "I lifted up my eyes and looked," Zech. 5:1
  9. "lift up your eyes and see," Zech. 5:5
  10. "I lifted up my eyes and looked," Zech. 5:9
  11. "I lifted up my eyes again and looked," Zech. 6:1

▣ "at night" Does this imply revelation by dreams or that a vision came in the night-time? God often used dreams to reveal Himself, especially in Genesis (cf. Gen. 20:3,6; 31:10-11,24; 37:5-20; 40-41). Dreaming even becomes a way of identifying a true prophet (cf. Deut. 13:1,3,5; Jer. 23:25-32).

The terms "dream" and "vision" can be synonymous (cf. Num. 12:6; Isa. 29:7; Dan. 1:12). However, they are distinct in 1 Sam. 28:6,15.

The most famous OT book which uses dreams and visions as a way of communicating truth is Daniel. Daniel's relation to Nebuchadnezzar II is very similar to Joseph's relation to Pharaoh. Dreams predominate in Daniel 1-7, while visions predominate in Daniel 8-11. Both are used by God to communicate truth.

Daniel and Zechariah share the apocalyptic element of dreams and angelic mediation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣ "a man" This is the Hebrew term ish (BDB 35), which usually denotes a male from a female (ishshah). The etymology of this word is uncertain because it is not found in the cognate languages.

In Zechariah it is used several times in the eight visions (cf. Zech. 1:8,10,21; 2:1; 4:1; 6:12), where it refers to:

  1. angels (compare Zech. 1:8,10 with 1:11)
  2. the prophet himself (cf. Zech. 4:1)
  3. the Messiah (i.e., Branch, cf. Zech. 6:12)

This same person is called "the angel of the Lord" in Zech. 1:11 and 12. For a good discussion of the different names for humans in the OT see Robert B. Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, pp. 45-54. Ish is discussed on pp. 48-50.

SPECIAL TOPIC: The Angel of the Lord

▣ "a red horse" The term "red" is the Hebrew term adam (BDB 10), which means reddish brown. Colored horses are also mentioned again in the eighth vision of Zechariah in 6:1-8. They become the source of the Apostle John's Four Horses of the Apocalypse (cf. Revelation 6). Notice that there are two red horses in Zech. 1:8 and no black horses.

▣
NASB  "and he was standing among the myrtle trees which were
  in the ravine"
NKJV  "and it stood among the myrtle trees in the hollow"
NRSV  "He was standing among the myrtle trees in a valley"
TEV  "he had stopped among some myrtle trees in a valley"
NJB  "standing among the deep-rooted myrtles"
REB, Peshitta  "the man standing among the myrtles"
JPSOA, LXX  "the man who stood among the shaded mountains"

From Zech. 1:11 it is possible that this is the angel of the Lord appearing as a man. He was also riding a red horse and standing among myrtle trees. There is debate as to how many angels appear in this vision. I think the man/angel on the red horse among the myrtle trees is different from the interpreting angel of Zech. 1:9,13,14.

Myrtle (BDB 213) seems to be imagery for joy and happiness. This was Esther's Jewish name, Hadassa. However, it may simply refer to a type of shrub growing near Jerusalem. See UBS Fauna and Flora of the Bible, pp. 149-150.

The LXX's "mountains" is very similar to "myrtles."

  1. myrtles ‒ ההרסים
  2. mountains ‒ ההרים

▣ "ravine" This Hebrew term (BDB 847, NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 1071) is possibly used as imagery for deep distress (BDB 846, same consonants, cf. Exod. 15:5; Zech. 10:11). Because of the apocalyptic nature of these visions it is possible that Zech. 1:8 speaks of God's people in peace (myrtle) and yet stress (ravine).

  1. BDB 847, KB 623 call the term "ravine" a rare, dubious word found only here. It is possible that it refers to a physical depression located near Jerusalem.
  2. JPSOA translates it as "in the Deep" (see SPECIAL TOPIC: DEEP)
  3. Peshitta as "gave shade" (see SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADOW AS IMAGERY FOR PROTECTION AND CARE)

If so, it is a way of showing God's care and presence with His people. Zechariah 1:11 seems to support this interpretation. These angels "patrolled the earth," but returned and stopped outside the holy city of Jerusalem, the place where YHWH's name dwells (i.e., Deut. 12:5,11,21; 14:23-24; 16:2,6,11; 26:2; Neh. 1:9).

▣ "red, sorrel and white horses" There seem to be four horses. Four is the number of the world (cf. Zech. 6:5-6; Rev. 7:1). This then would be a symbol of God's universal knowledge and presence.

There is an obvious parallel with Zech. 6:1-8 (also note Rev. 6:1-8). It has been noted that the names for the colors are PLURAL. Some commentators assume there were several of each color, not just three horses (or with the Septuagint, four adding a black one to match Zech. 6:1-8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #2

entries.title: Zechariah 1:9 "My lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:9 "My lord" This is not the covenant name for God, but simply the term adonai (BDB 10) for "my owner," "master," or "lord" (cf. Zech. 4:4,5,13). Zechariah is addressing his angel guide (cf. Zech. 1:19; 2:3; 4:1,4,5; 5:5,10; 6:4; also note a similar angel in Ezek. 8:2-3; 40:3-4; Dan. 7:16; 8:16-17; 9:22; 10:18-21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

▣ "I will show you" This angel does not tell Zechariah, but allows him to hear the angel on the red horse among the myrtles (cf. Zech. 1:11 and 12).

entries.title: Zechariah 1:10 "the man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 1:10 "the man" From Zech. 1:11 we believe that this was the angel of the Lord." We learn from Zech. 1:10 that these men on horses were angels who were patrolling the known world (cf. Zech. 6:5-7).

entries.title: Zechariah 1:11 "they answered the angel of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:11 "they answered the angel of the Lord" The phrase "the angel of the Lord" is often used in the OT for

  1. a powerful angel (cf. Gen. 24:7,40; Exod. 32:34; Num. 22:22; Jdgs. 5:23; 2 Sam. 24:16; 1 Chr. 21:15-16; Zech. 1:12-13)
  2. However, in other contexts it seems to refer to God Himself (cf. Gen. 16:7-13; 18:2,22; 22:11-15; 31:11,13; 48:15-16; Exod. 3:2-6; 13:21; 14:9; 20:20-23; Jdgs. 2:1; 6:14,22; 13:9-18,22; Zech. 3:1-2).
  3. Many have asserted that these passages refer to the pre-Incarnate Jesus.

It is obvious from Zech. 1:12 that the angel of the Lord is separate from the Lord of hosts. In Zech. 1:12 the angel prays an intercessory prayer to the Lord of hosts on behalf of the Jewish people (also note 1:10).

It seems to me that "the angel of the Lord" in Zech. 1:11 must be the same one speaking in 1:12.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ANGEL OF THE LORD

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts

▣
NASB  "all the earth is peaceful and quiet"
NKJV  "the earth is resting quietly"
NRSV  "the whole earth remains at peace"
REB, NJB  "whole earth at rest and in peace"
TEV  "the whole world lies helpless and subdued"
LXX  "all the earth is inhabited and at rest"
Peshitta  "all the earth sat and was silent"
NET  "everything is at rest and quiet"
JPSOA  "all the earth dwelling in tranquility"

This may refer to the enforced peace of the Persian Empire. We know from history that Dairus I Hystapes had to put down nineteen rebellions early in his reign. Apparently these were over and peace had been restored by force.

The TEV interprets "peaceful"(BDB 442, KB 444, QAL ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) and "quiet" (BDB 1052, KB 1641, QAL ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) as "helpless and subdued." It is translating the Hebrew words in a unique way based on context. The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1251, says "tranquility" carries a negative connotation. The interpretive question is, "What does the patrolling angel's answer mean?"

  1. all is quiet and well (cf. v. 15)
  2. all is not well, but quiet because Jerusalem and the temple had not been restored

Is the Persian Empire a liberating force or an occupying force? It seems to me that it is a liberating force, so different from Assyria and Babylon. It had allowed the Jews to return home and even offered funds and materials to rebuild their temple (as it did to other people groups also). In time it would allow the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem even amidst the objections of the surrounding nations (cf. Nehemiah). But, the returning Jews had not accomplished

  1. rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem
  2. finishing the rebuilding of the temple

entries.title: Zechariah 1:12 "the angel of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:12 "the angel of the Lord" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ANGEL OF THE LORD

▣ "how long will You have no compassion for Jerusalem and the cities of Judah" The angel (cf. Zech. 1:10,11) is addressing a question (or prayer) to YHWH about the extent of the exile. The angel is concerned about the lack of progress.

The Hebrew VERB "compassion" or "mercy" (BDB 933) is used in Hosea 1:6,19, and 23 as a word play between God's judgment (i.e., divorce) of His people and His promised renewal of the covenant.

The very fact that a prominent angel asked this question shows that the decree of Cyrus II in 538 B.C. to allow the Jews (along with all other captives) to return home was not the promised fulfillment which Jeremiah predicted. Zechariah addressed a discouraged people. The return had not been easy or blessed up to this point (519 B.C.).

Also note that an angel acting as an intermediary between YHWH and His people is surprising. It becomes a regular component of apocalyptic literature which magnifies the role of angels in human affairs. It also denotes that angels do not have a full knowledge of God's plans (i.e., Eph. 3:10; 1 Pet. 1:12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

▣ "these seventy years" This is an allusion to Jer. 25:11,12 and 29:10 (cf. 2 Chr. 36:21; Dan. 9:2), giving the specific time of the exile. There has been much discussion about this seventy year period. Is it meant to be a symbol of a large indefinite period of time, like the Hebrew term "forty" or is it a specific seventy year period? The two suggestions are

  1. the period from 605 B.C. (Battle of Carchemish) to 539 (fall of Babylon to Cyrus II)
  2. the seventy year period of time which can be found between the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in 586 B.C. to the rebuilding of the second temple in 516 B.C., which is the focus of the prophecy of both Haggai and Zechariah
  3. This same temporal symbol is also found in Isa. 23:15,17, where it seems to refer to one life span (which may be the intended thrust of the prophecy, much like "this generation" of the forty year Exodus judgment).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #4

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEVENTY YEARS

entries.title: Zechariah 1:13 "The Lord answered the angel who was speaking with me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:13 "The Lord answered the angel who was speaking with me" Notice YHWH does not answer the angel of the Lord among the myrtle trees who asked the question in Zech. 1:12, but He addresses the interpreting angel (cf. Zech. 1:9). The content of YHWH's gracious and comforting words is found in Zech. 1:14-17.

▣ "gracious words, comforting words" The first ADJECTIVE (BDB 373) means "good," "agreeable," or "pleasant." The second (BDB 637) means "compassion" (cf. Isa. 57:18; Hosea 11:8). God will forgive and restore His covenant people because of His great love and larger purposes, not their merit.

These ADJECTIVES answer the angel's question of "no compassion" in Zech. 1:12! YHWH has great compassion for His people and His restoration of the Abrahamic promise of the promised land (cf. Gen. 12:1-3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Zechariah 1:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:14 Zechariah 1:14-17 are the essence of the gracious words of YHWH mentioned in Zech. 1:13. They must be made known ("proclaim," BDB 894, KB 1128, Qal IMPERATIVE)!

▣ "I am exceedingly jealous for Jerusalem and Zion" This is a COGNATE ACCUSATIVE, like Zech. 1:2. "Exceedingly jealous" (BDB 888, KB 1109, NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 939) is from a term for dying a cloth an intense color. It came to be used for facial expressions showing deep emotions. Jealousy is a love word which speaks of the depth of God's compassion for the chosen people (cf. Exod. 20:5; Hosea 11:8; 13:14). For a good theological discussion of divine jealousy see Joyce Baldwin, Tyndale OT Commentaries, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, pp. 101-103.

The terms "Zion" and "Jerusalem" are often synonyms in the OT (e.g., Zech. 1:17; 2:7,10; 8:2,3; 9:9).

In light of the difficult historical setting (i.e., poor crops, poor relations with neighbors, and small group that returned) this is a surprising revelation. The returning minority was not sure that YHWH was with them or for them. It is so easy to judge spiritual issues based on physical circumstances.

SPECIAL TOPIC: JEALOUSY, ZEAL

SPECIAL TOPIC: MORIAH, SALEM, JEBUS, JERUSALEM, ZION

entries.title: Zechariah 1:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:15 This is a very significant verse. Although YHWH used godless nations to judge His people (cf. Isa. 10:5; 47:6; Jer. 25:9; 51:20), apparently these nations went far beyond what YHWH wanted and they themselves would be punished for their excesses. In the Ancient Near East military victory was a spiritual as well as military issue. YHWH explains why He allowed the pagan empires of Assyria and Babylon to oppress His people. He also explained that they went beyond His desires and purposes. The current conditions do not reflect YHWH's intended desires nor do they truly reflect His feelings for a restored Judah.

▣ "the nations who are at ease" This verse is the reason TEV translates Zech. 1:11c in a negative sense (also Jewish Study Bible, p 1251 and NET Bible, p. 1667, #2). The ADJECTIVE translated "ease" (BDB 983) has the added connotation of "careless, wanton, arrogant" ease (cf. Ps. 123:4; Isa. 32:9,11; Amos 6:1). The nations assumed YHWH would not judge them because He had not done so, so far (see NEB Bible footnote, #2, p. 1667). This second vision (cf. Zech. 1:18-21) expands this theme of YHWH's judgment on the very nations He used to punish His people.

▣
NASB, NIV, LXX   "I will return to Jerusalem"
NKJV   "I am returning to Jerusalem"
NRSV, NJB, REB, Peshitta   "I have returned to Jerusalem"
TEV   "I have come back to Jerusalem"
JPSOA   "I graciously return to Jerusalem"

The VERB (BDB 996, KB 1427) is a Qal PERFECT. The time element of Hebrew VERBS must be discerned from the context. Be careful of personal bias or systematic theology setting a particular time frame (only context can denote the original author's intent). The Jewish Publication Society of America's (JPSOA) translation supposes a current return. This is a play on the Hebrew word shub, used in Zech. 1:3,4,6. As they returned to YHWH, He would return to them. This is also significant because in Ezek. 10:18,19; 11:23, YHWH's presence left Jerusalem (the temple) and went east to be with the exiles. YHWH assures the returning Jews that His glory will return to a rebuilt temple and that the covenant would be reestablished (i.e., 516 B.C.).

▣ "with compassion" This is also a prophetic name play going back to Hosea 1:5-9; 2:1-7 versus 2:14-20,21-23 (i.e., Lo-Ruhamah = No Compassion; Lo-Ammi = Not My People).

▣ "and a measuring line will be stretched over Jerusalem" Usually this term meant destruction (cf. 2 Kgs. 21:13; Isa. 34:11; Lam. 2:8). In this context it must stand for "restoration" (BDB 876, cf. Zech. 2:1; Jer. 31:38-40; Ezek. 40-41; and Rev. 21:15-17). The use of building imagery references the emphasis on rebuilding the second temple.

entries.title: Zechariah 1:17 "Again, proclaim"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:17 "Again, proclaim" This parallels Zech. 1:14 (both Qal IMPERATIVES). The interpreting angel gives YHWH's words (cf. v. 13) in two parts: (1) restoration and (2) prosperity.

The word "again" (BDB 728) is repeated four times in this verse. That which was nullified or abrogated will be renewed and continued. The covenant is renewed!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

▣ "My cities will again overflow with prosperity" In this context YHWH is asserting that the destroyed cities of Judah will be rebuilt and prosper. This is an unusual use of this VERB (BDB 807 II, KB 918, Qal IMPERFECT). It usually is used in contexts of destruction and defeat (cf. Zech. 13:7). This may be a deliberate ambiguity implying that the "overflow" (cf. Prov. 15:6) or "expansion" of Judah's cities will be by military means.

This is a good place to remind us that context, not lexicons, determines meaning. It is always surprising when an exact opposite usage occurs, but this just shows the dynamic nature of human speech and the power of idiomatic language.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SPEECH

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE

▣ "again choose Jerusalem" This VERB (BDB 103, KB 119, Qal PERFECT with waw) is regularly used to denote a divine choice (cf. Zech. 2:12; 3:2). God has chosen to restore His chosen ones. This is official covenant renewal language.

Here Jerusalem and Zion are images, not for a city, but for a people. YHWH originally chose Jerusalem as the place for His name to dwell (cf. Deut. 12:5,11,21; 14:23-24; 16:2,6,11; 26:2; Neh. 1:9). This would be the location of the central sacrificial shrine.

entries.title: Zechariah 1:18 "Then I lifted up my eyes and looked"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:18 "Then I lifted up my eyes and looked" See note at Zech. 1:8. In the Masoretic Hebrew text Zech. 1:18 is 2:1 (cf. NJB).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT

▣ "four horns" Animal horns are symbolic of

  1. power
    1. military ‒ 2 Chr. 18:10; Ps. 92:10; Micah 4:13
    2. human strength ‒ 1 Sam. 2:1; 1 Kgs. 22:11; 1 Chr. 25:5; Job 16:15; Ps. 75:4,5,10; Ezek. 34:21
    3. divine strength ‒ 2 Sam. 22:3; Ps. 18:2; 112:10; 148:14; Jer. 48:25; Hab. 3:4
  2. nations
    1. nations ‒ Deut. 33:17; Ps. 89:17
    2. kings ‒ 1 Sam. 2:10; Ps. 89:24
    3. both ‒ Dan. 8:3,5,6,7,8,9,20,21; Zech. 1:18,19,21
  3. Messiah ‒ 1 Sam. 2:10; Ps. 132:17; Ezek. 29:21; Luke 1:69
  4. The horns on the incense and sacrificial altars were symbolic of power.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: ALTAR OF INCENSE
    SPECIAL TOPIC: ALTAR OF SACRIFICE

There is a good brief discussion on the use of "four" in biblical imagery in D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, pp. 115-116.

The number four seems to be the number of the world (i.e., four horses of Zech. 1:8 and the four winds of  Zech. 2:10). Some say that this refers to the kingdoms of Daniel, chapter 2 (Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #2

entries.title: Zechariah 1:19 "the angel who was speaking with me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:19 "the angel who was speaking with me" Angelic mediation (cf. Zech. 1:9) is one characteristic of apocalyptic literature, as is the use of symbolic numbers (cf. Zech. 1:18) and colors (cf. Zech. 1:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

▣ "These are the horns which have scattered Judah, Israel and Jerusalem" These horns (BDB 901) represent the world powers that YHWH used to judge ("scatter") His people (Egypt, Assyria, Babylon), but now He will judge ("scatter") them because of their excessively harsh treatment (cf. Zech. 1:15; Ps. 75:4-5).

This list of "Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem" is surprising in that Israel is usually listed first when speaking about the Divided Monarchy. If these refer to the two Jewish kingdoms formed after 922 B.C., why list the capital of Judah without the capital of Israel (i.e., Samaria)? It may be best to understand all three as collective terms for the people of God (only Judah is mentioned in Zech. 1:21).

1:20
NASB, NKJV, LXX   "craftsmen"
NRSV   "blacksmiths"
TEV   "workers with hammers"
NJB, REB, JPSOA   "smiths"
Peshitta   "carpenters"

YHWH's creative power is seen in His use of four craftsmen (BDB 360) versus the destructive power of human government seen in the imagery of four animal horns. It is uncertain if the craftsmen reflect artisans or workmen. Exactly what they do to the horns is unspecified, but they do change them and negate their power.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOVERNMENT

entries.title: Zechariah 1:21 "so that no man lifts up his head"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:21 "so that no man lifts up his head" This is an idiom of defeat and rejection. Notice the repeat of the term "lift up" (BDB 669, KB 724, Qal IMPERFECT with waw). YHWH's agents will reverse the roles, the scattering horns will be defeated and the defeated Jews' countenance will be lifted up!

There may be a word play on the phrase "throw down" (BDB 392), which can mean in the Hiphil, "give thanks," but in the Piel (here), "cast down." The horns who wanted to cast down the people of YHWH are now the focus of the praise and thanksgiving of the people to YHWH for the nations' defeat.

▣ "to scatter" The terms "scatter" (BDB 279, KB 280, Piel PERFECT of Zech. 1:19, 21[twice]) and "gather" were often used in the Ancient Near East as imagery for the well being of nations based on the activity of their gods. In the Bible it is YHWH who allowed His people to be scattered, but He will now protect them and gather them again.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why is Zechariah's father omitted in the list of priests in Zech. 1:1, but present in Ezra 5:1; 6:14; Neh. 12:4,16?
  2. Define the Hebrew word shub or "return."
  3. Who is the man riding on a red horse in Zech. 1:8?
  4. What is the significance of the colored horses in Zech. 1:8?
  5. Why is the angel upset in Zech. 1:12?
  6. What is the significance of Zech. 1:15 in our understanding of the exile?
  7. How does Zech. 1:16 fit the historical setting of Haggai and Zechariah?
  8. Explain the significance of "horns" in the OT.
  9. Who do the horns represent?

entries.title: Zechariah 2:1 "Then I lifted up my eyes and looked"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:1 "Then I lifted up my eyes and looked" See full note at Zech. 1:8. In the Masoretic Hebrew text this verse is Zech. 2:5 because the second vision (the four horns) starts chapter two.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT

▣ "a man" This apparently refers to an angelic being (BDB 35, ish, cf. Zech. 1:8,10 compared to 1:11,12). Angelic beings often appear as male humans (only once in Zech. 5:9 are they depicted as female).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

▣ "a measuring line" This is construction imagery (BDB 286 CONSTRUCT BDB 551, cf. Zech. 1:16). Another Hebrew word (BDB 876) with similar meaning is used for

  1. judgment/destruction (cf. 2 Kgs. 21:13; Isa. 34:11; Lam. 2:8)
  2. restoration (cf. Zech. 1:16; 2;1; Jer. 31:38-40; Ezek. 41; Rev. 21:15-17)
