READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This begins a new section of the book. Zechariah 9:2-11:3 is in a poetic format (NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NJB). As chapters 1- 8 are dated specifically and the author is specified (cf. Zech. 1:1), chapters 9-14 are undated and the author's name is not mentioned. This pattern is common in the prophetic books.
    1. Isaiah 1-39 and 40-66
    2. Ezekiel 1-39 and 40-48
    3. Daniel 1-6 and 7-12

  2. Zechariah chapters 1-8 are quoted often in the book of the Revelation, while Zechariah, chapters 9-14 are quoted often in the Gospels. Zechariah had an important theological message which still has relevance.

  3. This chapter, so it seems to me, depicts YHWH as invading Palestine from the north in an eschatological sense. His invasion is for spiritual renewal and reunification, not only of Judah and Israel, but also the surrounding ancient enemies (Hadrach, Syria, Phoenicia, and Philistia).

  4. It is possible from this passage to see YHWH coming in judgment in Zech. 9:1, 4-8. Many commentators see these verses as referring to Alexander's conquest of Syria, Phoenicia, and Philistia, but his sparing of Jerusalem in the early 330's B.C.. If this is so then Zech. 9:1 involves all men of the area watching the coming of Alexander as God's instrument of judgment.

  5. In his commentary on Zechariah H. C. Leupold assumes that Zech. 9:1-10 reflect the conquest of Alexander the Great of Palestine in the 330's B.C., while Zech. 9:11-17 reflect the Maccabean period, 168-165 B.C. The historical setting is uncertain; possibly it is a prophetic collage of:
    1. the past
    2. the post-exilic present
    3. the eschatological future

  6. There are dramatic theological-historical paradoxes in this chapter.
    1. destruction of the surrounding nations versus their inclusion in the covenant people
    2. the reference to peace in Zech. 9:8-10 versus a great war of Zech. 9:13-15
    3. the first coming of the Messiah in Zech. 9:9 versus the second coming of the Messiah in Zech. 9:10.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

9:1
NASB, NKJV  "The burden"
NRSV, REB  "An Oracle"
TEV  "message"
NJB  "a proclamation"
JPSOA  "A pronouncement"
LXX  "An issue"

This Hebrew term (BDB 672) is used in several senses.

  1. a load or burden carried by a donkey or camel (e.g., Isa. 46:1-2), used as imagery for people (e.g,. Num. 11:11,17; Deut. 1:12)
  2. Levites carrying the tabernacle (e.g., Num. 4:15,19,24,27,49) and, in worship, possibly Levitical singers lifting their voices
  3. a heavy prophetic utterance (e.g., Isa. 14:28; Jer. 23:33,34,38; Ezek. 12:10; Zech. 9:2; 12:1; Mal. 1:1)

Zechariah had a message from YHWH he had to deliver. There was a sense of urgency.

▣ "against" This is one of the meanings of this Hebrew PREPOSITION (BDB II 89, e.g., Gen. 16:12; 1 Sam. 3:9). The negative connotation to Zech. 9:1-2 is supported by 9:3-7. However, it is not the most common usage and probably if this was the author's intent, another Hebrew PREPOSITION would have been used (cf. USB, Handbook, pp. 229-230). Zechariah 9:1-2 seem very positive. YHWH's message was not only to Judah, but also to the surrounding nations. It was a message of hope and forgiveness (cf.Zech. 9:2,10).

▣ "Hadrach" Zechariah 9:1-4 deals with the northernmost geographical areas of the Promised Land (cf. Num. 34:1-12). This chapter depicts a spiritual invasion by YHWH beginning in the north and moving south. This first term, Hadrach, appears only here in the OT. It referred to:

  1. a district near Damascus
  2. a city in North Syria mentioned in the Assyrian documents (see IVP Bible Background Commentary [OT], p. 804)

▣ "Damascus" This was the capital of Syria, Israel's traditional northern enemy (cf. Jer. 49:23-27).

▣ "as its resting place" This Hebrew term (BDB 629) could mean that

  1. YHWH's word is focused on His people's enemies
  2. YHWH's word was resting or abiding in Damascus

The term does not have a negative connotation (e.g., 2 Sam. 14:17; Isa. 32:18). It is even used of YHWH's resting place in 2 Chr. 6:41 and Ps. 132:8. It is also used in connection with the nations coming to Him in Isa. 11:10.

▣
NASB, NKJV, NIV  "for the eyes of men"
NRSV, REB  "the capital of Aram"
TEV  "the capital of Syria"
NJB  "for the source of Aram"
NAB  "for the cities of Aram"
JPSOA  "for all men's eyes"
LXX  "the Lord oversees people"
Peshitta  "the ways of men"

This phrase is literally "the eye of man" ("Adam," BDB 9). The focus and attention of

  1. all human creation will be on the covenant-making God, as well as His covenant people (cf. Zech. 8:20-23)
  2. YHWH's care and desire for all humans to know Him and serve Him (cf. Zech. 9:10)
  3. the inhabitants of the Ancient Near East, especially Palestine, are involved in Alexander the Great's conquest. He was an instrument in the hand of God (The Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 7, pp. 657-658)

The NRSV and TEV translations require textual changes to arrive at their wording (Adam to Aram with the addition of "the capital of").

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Zechariah 9:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:2 The NKJV adds the word "against" from Zech. 9:1 here (twice) assuming the context refers to punishment, but TEV links this verse with the phrase "belong to the Lord" (cf. NJB, Zech. 9:1) and thereby turns it into an affirmation of YHWH's love for the nations. The context, especially Zech. 9:4, favors NKJV's understanding.

▣ "Hamath" This is a city in the northern part of the Promised Land, which is mentioned in 2 Kgs. 14:28. It is often depicted as the northern-most limit of God's geographical covenant with Abraham (cf. Num. 13:21; 34:1-12; Josh. 13:5; Jdgs. 3:3). See IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), pp. 804-5.

▣ "Tyre and Sidon, though they are very wise" This refers to the Phoenician coastal cities mentioned in Ezek. 28:3-5,7 as being proverbially wise. However, judgment came on them because of their pride (cf. Ezek. 28:2,5-6) and arrogance (cf. Ezek. 28:2,6,9).

Now, the contextual question returns, is this context positive (the nations turn to YHWH) or negative (YHWH judges the nations)? The Hebrew CONJUNCTION (BDB 453-455) in Zech. 9:2b has many possible meanings. The TEV has "with"; REB has "for," not "though." Phoenicia was the source of artisans who designed and built Solomon's temple (cf. 1 Kgs. 7:13-14; 2 Chronicles 2). This could be the intent of the phrase "they are very wise."

When we look at the following context the same paradox of blessing and cursing repeats itself. It is obvious that Zech. 9:3-6 are negative, but look at Zech. 9:7-10!

entries.title: Zechariah 9:3 "Tyre. . .fortress"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:3 "Tyre. . .fortress" There is a play on the Hebrew word for "Tyre," which is sor (BDB 862), and the Hebrew word for fortress, masor ("rampart" or "siege work" BDB 848). There was an old city of Tyre and a new Tyre. New Tyre was an island fortress about a half-mile off the coast, with walls over 150 feet high. It was besieged by several Assyrian kings and finally fell to Shelmanezzar V after a five-year siege. It was besieged by Nebuchadnezzar II, but after thirteen years it was never taken, Ezek. 29:18, implies that he gave up. It fell to Alexander the Great in 322 B.C.. in a seven-month siege. Many commentators speculate that this chapter reflects Alexander the Great's conquest of Palestine in the 330's B.C. as he moved toward Egypt because:

  1. he destroyed the old Tyre and used the rubble to build a causeway to the island fortress (cf. Zech. 9:4b)
  2. he destroyed the island fortress with fire (cf. Zech. 9:4c)

▣ "And piled up silver like dust and gold like the mire of the streets" This is figurative language reflecting the commercial power of the city of Tyre from their extensive maritime activities (cf. Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 27).

9:4
NASB  "the Lord will dispossess her"
NKJV  "the Lord will cast her out"
NRSV  "the Lord will strip it of its possessions"
TEV  "the Lord will take away everything she has"
NJB  "the Lord is going to dispossess her"
LXX  "the Lord will possess it"
Peshitta  "the Lord will destroy her"

There is irony here. The Hebrew term (BDB 439, KB 441, Hiphil IMPERFECT) means to inherit, but in certain contexts in the Hiphil stem can mean dispossess or disinherit (e.g., Num 14:12). YHWH wants to include the nations into His family and give them an inheritance, but they must turn from idolatry and materialism and trust in Him.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

▣
NASB, NRSV, TEV, Peshitta  "cast her wealth into the sea"
NKJV  "will destroy her power in the sea"
NJB  "at sea he will break her power"
NET  "shove her fortifications into the sea"
REB  "will break her power at sea"
JPSOA  "will defeat her forces at sea"
LXX  "will strike its power into the sea"

The question is over the OBJECT of the VERB.

  1. wealth (BDB 298 #3, cf. Zech. 14:14)
  2. power (BDB 298 #1)
  3. fortifications

The NET Bible (p. 1672) asserts that the form can reflect the word "fortress" and that the chiastic structure supports this root. Alexander the Great used the rubble of the old city of Tyre to reach the island fortress and then threw (BDB 645, KB 697, Hiplil PERFECT with waw, "hurl") its walls into the ocean (332 B.C.)

However, as the UBS Handbook notes (p. 234) the Hebrew term can refer to sea power (cf. NKJV, NAB, REB, NIV). Sea power was the source of Phoenicia's wealth and power.

▣ "she will be consumed with fire" This VERB (BDB 37, Niphal IMPERFECT) means "devoured." This was predicted in Amos 1:9-10 (cf. Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26) and fulfilled by Alexander the Great in 332 B.C.

entries.title: Zechariah 9:5 "Askelon. . .Gaza. . .Ekron. . .Ashdod"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:5 "Askelon. . .Gaza. . .Ekron. . .Ashdod" These are four of the five city states of the Philistines (NIDOTTE, vol. 3, pp. 631-634) in the Promised Land (Gath was earlier destroyed by the Assyrians). The Philistines invaded Egypt around the 1200's, but were defeated and then settled in the southern coastal areas of Palestine. They were apparently of the same racial stock as the Phoenicians, possibly from Cypress or the Aegean Islands. They are the only uncircumcised people in Canaan and were traditional enemies of the people of God (cf. Judges, 1 Samuel). Because of Zech. 9:5-7b, although they are going to be judged, they are also going to be included in the covenant people (cf. Zech. 9:7c-d). What a surprising message of grace!

▣
NASB, NRSV, Peshitta  "will see it and be afraid"
NKJV  "shall see it and fear"
TEV  "will see this and be afraid"
NJB  "seeing this. . .will be terrified"
LXX  "will see and be afraid"

The NASB has "it" italicized, which means that the word does not appear in the Hebrew text. From the immediate context, "it" must refer to the siege and utter destruction of the powerful city of Tyre.

Zechariah 9:5 may be an allusion to the prophecy of destruction in Amos 1:6-8 (esp. Zech. 9:8).

▣ "will writhe in great pain" This Hebrew term (BDB 296, KB 297, Qal IMPERFECT) is used of childbirth (e.g., Isa. 26:12; 45:10) and became an idiom for judgment (cf. Isa. 13:8; Jer. 30:7; Micah 4:9-10; Matt. 24:8; Mark 13:8; Acts 2:24; 1 Thess. 5:3). This fear and pain was brought on by the destruction of Tyre, Philistia's northern ally. With Phoenicia conquered by Greece, Philistia was next!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIRTH PAINS

▣ "Ekron" We learn from Josh. 15:45-47, that Ekron, Ashdod, and Gaza were considered to be in the tribal allocation of Judah and were its traditional enemy!

▣
NASB  "her expectation has been confounded"
NKJV  "He dried up her expectation"
NRSV  "its hopes are withered"
TEV  "her hopes will be shattered"
NJB  "at the ruin of her prospects"
JPSOA  "at the collapse of her hopes"
LXX  "because it was put to shame by its transgression"
Peshitta  "because her hopoe is confounded"

There is confusion of whether this Hiphil VERB is "be ashamed" (BDB 101, KB 116, Hiphil PERFECT, cf. Zech. 10:5) or "be dried up" (BDB 386, KB 384).

The second one is found in Zech. 10:11 (Hiphil) and 11:17 (Qal). However, Joel, which I think is early post-exilic, also has four places where these same two roots are confused (Joel 1:10,12 [twice] and 17).

If "be ashamed" is adopted then the idiom reflects defeat in battle (cf. 10:5; 2 Kgs. 19:26; Isa. 37:27; 41:11; Jer. 46:24; 48:20; 50:11-16; 51:45-58; Ezek. 32:30; Micah 7:16), which fits this context.

entries.title: Zechariah 9:6 "a mongrel race"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:6 "a mongrel race" This (BDB 561) seems to refer to the Assyrian exile of the Jewish people from Israel (722 B.C.) and the import of pagan people from Media; therefore, this area was populated by people of mixed national origins.

The rabbis later use this term (BDB 561, an Aramaic word for incest) to describe a child of the union between a Jew and a pagan (cf. Deut. 23:2-3) or to a child born of rape or incest.

▣ "I will cut off the pride of the Philistines" In this VERB (BDB 503, KB 500, Hiphil PERFECT) there is a change from the THIRD PERSON to the FIRST PERSON. This is common in prophecy as YHWH begins to speak for Himself through the prophet.

As YHWH overthrew Phoenicia (Tyre and Sidon) because of their pride (cf. Zech. 9:2-4; Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 27-28), so too, Philistia and also Egypt (cf. Ezek. 30:18; 32:12) and Assyria (cf. Zech. 10:11).

entries.title: Zechariah 9:7 "I will remove their blood from their mouth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:7 "I will remove their blood from their mouth" This may mean that the Philistines will keep the Jewish food laws (cf. Leviticus 11; 17:10-16; Deuteronomy 14) and, thereby be YHWH's people. Even His people were accused of eating forbidden, bloody meat (cf. Ezek. 33:25), which violated the Levitical laws. They were destroyed (cf. Ezek. 33:27-28), but these uncircumcised pagans will be saved.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOOD LAWS

▣ "then they also will be a remnant for our God" The concept of "remnant" (BDB 983) is a very important historical and theological concept. The multiple uses can be seen in the New International Dictionary of Old Testament Theology and Exegesis, vol. 4, p. 15.

  1. those who survived a divine catastrophe (e.g., Philistines, cf. Amos 1:8; Jer. 47:4 and Jews, cf. Isa. 37:4,31-32; 40:11; 42:2; Jer. 25:20)
  2. those who remain faithful and obedient to YHWH (e.g., Isa. 10:20-22; Amos 5:15; Micah 5:3,7,8)
  3. those who form the eschatological people of God (e.g., Amos 9:12; Jer. 23:3; 31:7; Isa. 11:11,16)

This is a very strong statement for the inclusion of these hated Philistine enemies who now are also part of the faithful remnant! Some see this prophecy fulfilled in the ministry of Philip in Acts 8:26-40.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT (three senses)

▣
NASB, NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB, JPSOA  "and be like a clan in Judah"
NKJV  "shall be like a leader of Judah"
LXX  "shall be like an officer in Judah"
Peshitta  "shall be like the princes of Judah"
UBS Text Project, p. 411  "like a friend"

The Hebrew term (BDB 48-49) is literally "thousands." It is used in several senses.

  1. literally (e.g., Gen. 20:16; Exod. 32:28)
  2. family units or leaders (e.g., Josh. 22:14; Jdgs. 6:15; 1 Samuel 23; Zech. 9:7)
  3. military units or leaders (e.g., Exod. 18:21,25; Deut. 1:15)
  4. symbolically (e.g., Gen. 24:60; Exod. 20:6; 34:7; Deut. 7:9; Jer. 32:18)

The difference between NKJV and the others is only vocalization (i.e., vowel points added by Masoretic scholars). The ancient versions (Septuagint and Vulgate) translated it as "leader," but most modern English translations have "clan" (cf. Zech. 12:5-6). The NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 407, labels it "Philistine leaders." The contextual issue is not leadership, but covenant inclusion. This inclusion is all the more shocking when the traditional enemy of Judah becomes part of Judah!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND

▣ "Ekron like a Jebusite" The Jebusites were the original Canaanite inhabitants of the city of Jebus, also called Salem (cf. Genesis 14), and later called Jerusalem. When David finally defeated their stronghold (cf. 2 Sam. 5:6-10; 1 Chr. 11:45-9) he did not relegate them to the sword, but allowed them to live (cf. Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21; 1 Kings 9:20-21). This Philistine city is now included into the very heart of Judah—Jerusalem.

SPECIAL TOPIC: JEBUS

entries.title: Zechariah 9:8 "But I will camp around My house"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:8 "But I will camp around My house" The VERB (BDB 333, KB 332) is a Qal PERFECT with waw. This may be an allusion to Zech. 2:5 (cf. Ps. 34:7-8), which speaks of YHWH's protecting His people (cf. Isa. 60:15-22) in a military sense. The Promised Land had been invaded again and again because of its strategic location, but there will come a day when YHWH will personally indwell and protect the Promised Land (cf. Ps. 34:7).

▣
NASB  "because of an army"
NKJV  "because of the army"
NRSV, NET  "as a guard"
TEV  "I will guard my land and keep armies from passing through it"
NJB  "to defend it against all comers"
REB  "post a garrison"
JPSOA  "will encamp"
LXX  "set up a structure"
Peshitta  "cause to dwell"

The BDB Lexicon (663) speculates that this form, which is found only here, is from one of two roots, "to stand guard" or "to garrison" (BDB 662, cf. NRSV and TEV). However, it also mentions that the MT notes (Qere) suggest that it may come from another term, "because of a host" or "because of an army" (NASB, NKJV).

YHWH will protect His new temple.

▣ "For now I have seen with My eyes" There will be no more invasions of the Promised Land because of YHWH's personal presence and power (cf. Deut. 11:12). This idiom of His all-knowing presence possibly refers to Zech. 4:10.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

entries.title: Zechariah 9:9 "Rejoice greatly"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:9 "Rejoice greatly" This (BDB 162, KB 189, plus ADVERB 547) is a Qal IMPERATIVE (cf. Zech. 2:10; Zeph. 3:14,15). This is a shout of joy over the military conquest by YHWH's Messiah. This rejoicing includes both Jews and Gentiles (cf. Zech. 2:10-13). This inclusion is so surprising and unexpected (cf. Zeph. 3:14-20).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "O daughter of Zion" This idiomatic phrase (see notes at Amos 5:2 and Jer. 46:11) is often used in judgment passages, but here is an allusion to the love that YHWH has for the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

▣ "Shout in triumph" This (BDB 929, KB 1206) is a Hiphil IMPERATIVE. This phrase is parallel to "rejoice greatly."

▣ "Behold, your king is coming to you" The VERB (BDB 97, KB 112) is a Qal IMPERFECT. This is one of many quotes in the Gospels which comes from this section of Zechariah. It is used in the Gospels for Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem (cf. Matt. 21:5; John 12:15). For the concept of YHWH and the Messiah as King see 1 Sam. 8:7; 12:12.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KINGDOM OF GOD

▣
NASB  "He is just and endowed with salvation"
NKJV, LXX  "He is just and having salvation"
NRSV  "triumphant and victorious is he"
TEV  "He comes triumphant and victorious"
NJB  "he is vindicated and victorious"
REB  "his cause won, his victory gained"
JPSOA  "He is victorious, triumphant"
Peshitta  "He is righteous and a Saviour"

This first term "just" or "righteous" (BDB 841-843) seems to be used in several passages in the prophets to describe the ethical reign of the Messiah (cf. Isa. 9:7; 11:4,5; 16:5; 32:1; Jer. 23:5-6). The Messiah is called "the Righteous One" in the Suffering Servant song of Isa. 53:11. He is qualified to reign by lineage and actions.

The term "salvation" (BDB 446, KB 448) is a Niphal PARTICIPLE used in the sense of someone who is made victorious or someone who is delivered. Both of these terms are used together in Isa. 45:8; 46:13; 51:4,5.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TITLES FOR THE SPECIAL COMING ONE

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT Term)

▣ "Humble" This word (BDB 776) is used in several ways in Zechariah:

  1. in the sense of "afflicted" (cf. Zech. 11:7,11; Isa. 14:32; 49:13; 51:21; 54:11) or "poor" (cf. Zech. 7:10; Isa. 3:14-15; 10:30; 11:4; 32:7; 41:17; 58:7; 61:1). "Afflicted" describes the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53, although Zech. 9:2 and 3 use a different term. Isaiah 53:7 uses the same root (BDB 776 III)
  2. here, it is the sense of "lowly" or "meek" (e.g., Prov. 16:19)

▣ "and mounted on a donkey, even on a colt the foal of a donkey" Donkeys were the royal mount of Israeli kings (cf. 2 Sam. 13:29; 16:2; 18:9;1 Kgs. 1:33-34, 38,44). They were a symbol of royalty, however, the colt of a donkey was used because only the king could ride on this donkey. Therefore, this would be the first time the colt had been ridden. This entire verse reflects Gen. 49:8-12, which is a prophecy about the tribe of Judah, but is also a description of the coming Messiah. He will be

  1. of the royal line of Judah (cf. 2 Samuel 7)
  2. humble
  3. a suffering servant (cf. Isaiah 53)

The Gospel writers saw this fulfilled in Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem (cf. Matt. 21:4-9; Mark 11:7-10; Luke 19:35-38; John 12:12-15).

entries.title: Zechariah 9:10 "And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:10 "And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim" Zechariah 9:9 speaks of Christ's triumphal entry into Jerusalem, while 9:10 describes the Second Coming. Also notice

  1. YHWH speaks (cf. Zech. 9:6,8) in Zech. 9:10a-c
  2. the Messiah is spoken of in Zech. 9:10d-f

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARIOTS

▣ "And he will speak peace to the nations" This latter part of Zech. 9:10 seems to reflect Ps. 72:8-11, where the peace of Palestine is used in a universal sense of the reign of the Messiah. However, it is significant that the Messiah will speak peace to all the nations as well as the Jews (e.g., Zech. 8:20-23; Isa. 2:2-4; Micah 4:1-3; 5:4). This surprising, yet prophesied inclusion (cf. Gen. 12:3; 18:18; 22:16; Exod. 19:5), is the ultimate fulfillment of Gen. 3:15, which relates to all humanity, not only the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ The last two poetic lines of Zech. 9:10 are parallel in the ideal limits of the Promised Land (cf. Exod. 23:31; Num. 34:1-12; 1 Kgs. 4:21). "The River" refers to the head waters of the Euphrates.

The phrase "sea to sea" does not seem to fit the universal thrust of this context. Therefore, it is possible to relate it to "the cosmic ocean," which is universal ANE imagery. See IVP Bible Background Commentaryr (OT), p. 805 (Zech. 9:10 two items).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

▣ "to the ends of the earth" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND COUNTRY, EARTH

entries.title: Zechariah 9:11 "the blood of My covenant"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:11 "the blood of My covenant" This is a CONSTRUCT of BDB 196 and 136. This can refer either to

  1. the original covenant of YHWH with Abraham mentioned in Gen. 15:9-11
  2. the Mosaic covenant in Exod. 24:8
  3. This phrase is also used by Jesus in the Upper Room in Mark 14:24.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "I have set your prisoners free from the waterless pit" The VERB (BDB 1018, KB 1511) is a Piel PERFECT. Apparently this is imagery describing the Jewish exiles returning from Mesopotamia (cf. Isa. 24:22; 51:14).

entries.title: Zechariah 9:12 "Return"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:12 "Return" This is a Qal IMPERATIVE. Zechariah 9:11 and 12 both are encouragement to the returning remnant (cf. Ezra and Nehemiah). Very few of the Jews in exile ever returned to Palestine.

This term (BDB 996, KB 1427), however, is often used for repentance (cf. Zech. 1:3,4). YHWH's people must return to Him, not just to a geographical location or even to an ancient promise. Biblical faith is personal.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

▣
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta  "the stronghold"
NRSV  "your stronghold"
TEV  "your place of safety"
NJB  "the fortress"
JPSOA  "Bizzaron"
REB  "citadel"

This term (BDB 131; NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 701-2) is found only here in the OT. Its basic root means

  1. "is cut off" (used of grapes)
  2. "inaccessible" (used most often for fortifications, e.g., Zeph. 1:16)
  3. "fortress by enclosure" (cf. Isa. 22:10)

The TEV takes it as imagery for God's care and protection in the Promised Land (cf. Jer. 16:19; Joel 3:16).

The JPSOA, in its footnote, thinks it is a nickname ("fortress") for Samaria, the northern capital of Israel destroyed in 722 B.C. by Assyria.

▣
NASB  "prisoners who have the hope"
NKJV, JPSOA  "you prisoners of hope"
NRSV  "O prisoners of hope"
TEV  "you exiles who now have hope"
NJB, REB  "you prisoners wiating in hope"
LXX  "O prisoners of the gathering"
Peshitta  "O you prisoners of the congregation"

The hope is in the covenant-making (cf. Zech. 9:11), promise-keeping, deliverance-giving God. This phrase is given either to encourage those who have returned or to motivate others to return (NJB).

▣ "I will restore double to you" The VERB (BDB 996, KB 1427, Hiphil IMPERFECT) is an idiom for something that is complete and full. It can relate to YHWH's judgment (cf. Isa. 40:2; Jer. 16:18) or YHWH's promise of restoration (cf. Isa. 61:7). YHWH is just and acts according to His word.

entries.title: Zechariah 9:13 "I will bend Judah as My bow"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:13 "I will bend Judah as My bow" This chapter is filled with paradoxes! The coming Messianic peace is mentioned in Zech. 9:8-11 and yet 9:13 speaks again of war (BDB 201, KB 231 Qal PERFECT). Possibly this verse shows the promise of Zech. 9:8!

As Zech. 9:10 mentioned "Ephraim" and "Jerusalem," which denotes Israel and Judah, so too, Zech. 9:13a,b. The divided kingdom will be reunited! As a bow and arrow are used as one instrument, so too, God's reunited people (cf. Zech. 10:4d).

▣ "'I will stir'" The term (BDB 734 I, KB 802, Polel PERFECT) is used several times in Zechariah.

  1. YHWH is aroused from His holy habitation, Zech. 2:13
  2. the interpreting angel wakes the prophet, Zech. 4:1 (twice)
  3. YHWH arouses the inhabitants of Zion against the Greeks, Zech. 9:13
  4. YHWH arouses His sword against His own Shepherd, Zech. 13:7

Two other prophets use this same term in connection with Greece, Dan. 11:2 and Joel 3:6. Isaiah uses this term often in connection with God directing the history of His people (e.g., "the Medes," Isa. 13:17; "one from the east," Isa. 41:2; "one from the north," Isa. 41:25; "Cyrus," Isa. 45:13; "Jerusalem and Zion," Isaiah 51; 52). Isaiah's use of this term in chapters 51 and 52 may parallel Zech. 9:13d, "I will make you like a warrior's sword." It is God's strength and purpose, but He chooses to use human instrumentality.

▣ "O Zion, against your sons, O Greece" The term here for Greece is Jawan or Javan, which was used originally in the OT for a descendant of Japheth (cf. Gen. 10:2,4; Isa. 66:19), while in Isa. 66:19 it is used for a nation. In the books of Daniel and Joel, it is used to designate Greece (cf. Dan. 8:21; 10:20; Joel 3:6). I agree with Joyce Baldwin, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries, that it is used in its Genesis 10 sense of a distant people on the fringe of civilization, which is how it is used in this eschatological context (cf. p. 169).

entries.title: Zechariah 9:14 "Then the Lord will appear over them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:14 "Then the Lord will appear over them" The VERB (BDB 906, KB 1157, Niphal IMPERFECT) may be an allusion to the promise of protection in Zech. 2:5 (cf. Zech. 9:8a). It also may be an allusion to Isa. 31:5, where God is a protecting bird of prey (cf. Exod. 19:4b) or a mother bird hovering overhead (cf. Deut. 32:11; Ps. 91:4). The third possibility is borrowing the imagery of Assyria where their god fluttered over his troops in battle.

Zechariah 9:14-17 are the hyperbolic language of theophany. The phrases are reminiscent of other prophetic texts. They are patterned, standard idioms of the ANE (see Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, D. Brent Sandy).

▣ "His arrows will go forth like lightning" Lightning (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 769) and arrows are often used as imagery for YHWH's fighting on behalf of His people (cf. Ps. 18:14; 144:6; Hab. 3:11). The concept of YHWH's arrows being like lightning is found in Ps. 7:12-13, where it may refer to arrows set on fire to incinerate wooden defenses.

▣ "the Lord God" This is the combination of the Hebrew term YHWH (BDB 217) and adon (BDB 10). Because it would be repetitive in English to say "Lord, LORD," when these two terms appear together (so too, YHWH and Elohim, e.g., Zech. 9:16 and Gen. 2:4). They are translated, "Lord God."

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C., D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

▣ "blow the trumpet" "Trumpet" (shofar) has an uncertain etymology. It came to be used in Hebrew for a ram's horn (BDB 1051; NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 68). The rabbis designated it to be made (softened and lengthened by soaking it in water) from the left horn of a male goat. It is used for

  1. military purposes, Josh. 6:4,5,20; Jdgs. 7:8,16
  2. religious purposes, Exod. 19:13,16,19; Lev. 25:9; 2 Sam. 6:15; 2 Chr. 15:14; Ps. 81:3; 98:6; 150:3
  3. information gathering (usually about military matters), Jdgs. 3:27; 6:34; 1 Sam. 13:3
  4. coronation of a king, 1 Kgs. 1:34,39; Ps. 47:5
  5. invasion of the land, Jer. 4:5; 6:1; Hosea 5:8; 8:1; Joel 2:1; Amos 2:2; 3:6; Zeph. 1:16

Notice in this context it is YHWH who blows (i.e., "sounds," BDB 1075, Qal IMPERFECT) the trumpet (cf. Isa. 27:13; Matt. 24:31; 1 Cor. 15:52; 1 Thess. 4:16; Rev. 11:15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORNS USED BY ISRAEL

▣ "the storm winds of the south" This could be a reference to

  1. the Siniatic covenant (cf. Exodus 24)
  2. God's presence as a desert storm (cf. Isa. 29:6; Ezek. 1:4; 13:11,13)
  3. "the south" being the antonym to "the north," which was imagery for invasion

The south is often imagery for salvation and deliverance (cf. Jdgs. 5:4-5; Hab. 3:3).

entries.title: Zechariah 9:15 "The Lord of hosts will defend them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:15 "The Lord of hosts will defend them" God Himself will act on His people's behalf. His victory is their victory. The term "hosts" in this context would refer to the angelic army at YHWH's command. See SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

The VERB "defend" (BDB 170, KB 199, Hiphil IMPERFECT) can be translated "cover," "surround," or "defend" (cf. Zech. 12:8). In Isa. 31:5 it is used of a mother bird protecting her young (cf. Deut. 32:11; Ps. 91:4). Here it is used as a shield protecting the soldiers from projectiles.

▣ "the sling stones" These were stones used in sling weapons (BDB 887 I; NIDOTTE, vol. 3, pp. 930-932) which were used to defend cities and forts (cf. Jdgs. 20:16; 1 Sam. 17:40,50; 2 Chr. 26:14; Job 41:28). This is imagery for the complete destruction of a military foe.

▣ "they will drink and be boisterous as with wine" Both VERBS (BDB 1059, KB 1667 and BDB 242, KB 250) are Qal PERFECTS. This refers to the victory celebration of God's soldiers (cf. Ps. 78:65).

The UBS Text Project, p. 413, gives three options for this phrase.

  1. "and they will drink, roar" ‒ ושׁתו המו
  2. "and they will drink their blood" ‒ ושׁתו דמם
  3. "and they will drink blood" ‒ שׁתו דם

It gives a "C" rating to option #1. The VERB (BDB 242, KB 250, Qal PERFECT can mean

  1. be turbulent
  2. growl
  3. murmur

Jews would be appalled at the thought of "drinking blood" (some LXX MSS) but they would be well aware of loud military victory parties!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

▣ "filled like a sacrificial basin" English translations differ on how to understand these last two poetic lines. They seem to refer to the previous line about God's people rejoicing with wine over His victory (i.e., another Qal PERFECT with waw VERB, BDB 569, KB 583). The wine reminded our author about

  1. the blood of the slain enemies, captured in a bowl
  2. blood as an aspect of sacrifice to YHWH

The corners of the altar are where the blood in the bowl was poured out at the base of the altar of sacrifice.

YHWH made a blood covenant with the descendants of Abraham (cf. Zech. 9:11). Now He defends them by spilling the blood of their enemies.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SACRIFICIAL ALTAR

entries.title: Zechariah 9:16 "the Lord their God will save them in that day"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:16 "the Lord their God will save them in that day" This is parallel to the opening lines of Zech. 9:14 and 15. As 9:14 had Adon YHWH, this verse has YHWH Elohim.

The term "save" (BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil PERFECT) includes several connotations from the context:

  1. military victory
  2. spiritual renewal and inclusion
  3. God's personal care, protection, and provision

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT TERM)

▣ "As the flock of His people" This whole section of Zechariah reflects Jer. 31:10-14. God is the shepherd (e.g. Psalm 23) who acts on behalf of His flock. Later in this section of Zechariah the Messiah will be described as the wounded shepherd (cf. chapters 12-13) and His people as the afflicted flock (cf. chapter 11).

▣ "as the stones of a crown" This may be

  1. a contrast to the sling stones mentioned in Zech. 9:15
  2. an allusion to Isa. 62:3, the precious stones used to describe God's people
  3. an allusion to the coronation of the new king (the Messiah as YHWH's representative)
▣
NASB  "Sparkling in His land"
NKJV  "Lifted like a banner over His land"
NRSV  "they shall shine on his land"
TEV  "they will shine in his land"
NJB  "sparkle over his country"
REB  "which sparkle all about his land"
JPSOA  "like crown jewels glittering on His soil"
LXX  "sacred stones roll on his land"
Peshitta  "for they were holy stones cast upon his land"

The VERB in the Hithpoel stem is rare and ambiguous.

  1. BDB ‒ "to be high," "conspicuous," "prominent" (BDB 651 II)
  2. Lexicon, William Holladay, "rally around the banner" (p. 240). This comes from Ps. 60:4, which may refer to Exod. 17:15 or possibly Isa. 62:10.
  3. KB ‒ "to assemble under the banner" (KB 704)
  4. "sparkle," "glitter," "shine" are the most common English translations (cf. Isa. 62:3)

entries.title: Zechariah 9:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:17 As the previous verses may be an allusion to Jer. 31:10-11, so too, this may refer to the return from exile, but extends it to the eschatological future and the time of the "new covenant" (cf. Jer. 31:31-34).

The promised days of abundance and stability for an obedient covenant people (cf. Lev. 26 and Deut. 27-29; Ezek. 36:22-36) have now been realized by the gracious actions of YHWH, not human performance (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why is this chapter so difficult to place in its historical setting?
  2. Does this chapter refer to the judgment of pagan nations or to their inclusion in the covenant people?
  3. Is there a definite historical separation between Zech. 9:1-10 and Zech. 9:11-17? Why?
  4. Explain the Messianic elements in Zech. 9:9 and show their NT counterpoints.
  5. To whom does Javan refer? Why is the nation mentioned?

entries.title: Zechariah 10:1 "Ask rain"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:1 "Ask rain" This is a Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 981, KB 1371). Rain was a gift from God, e.g., Isa. 30:23; Jer. 10:13; Joel 2:23). The emphasis of Zech. 1:17; 9:17 is on social stability and fruitfulness being from YHWH. Famine was part of the curse of Deuteronomy 28 (cf. Jer. 14:1-6), but abundant rain was also part of the promised blessing if they followed God (cf. Deut. 11:13,14; 28:12). During Israel's periods of idolatry (e.g., Hosea 4) she ascribed fertility to Ba'al (Canaanite storm and fertility god) and not to YHWH (cf. Jer. 14:22). Chapter 10 highlights this grave mistake (cf. Zech. 14:17).

The VERB "ask" refers to prayer. This is theologically parallel to "seek." These acts of repentant worship were done at YHWH's sanctuary. YHWH's people were not to "ask" and "seek" Ba'al but Him. He and He alone was the provider of covenant promises, blessings!

▣ "at the time of the spring rain" In Palestine there are only two periods of rain (cf. Deut. 11:14; Jer. 5:24; Joel 2:23).

  1. early rain at the autumn time before spring planting (October ‒ November)
  2. latter rain at the time of the maturing plant (March ‒ April)

Most regular moisture comes from the heavy dew. Because of the covenant promises and cursing of Lev. 26 and Deut. 27-29, these periods of rain became imagery for spiritual renewal and the presence of YHWH with His people for blessing.

The "latter rains" became an idiom for YHWH's blessing in the end-time (e.g., Hosea 6:3; Joel 2:23).

▣
NASB, NRSV, NJB, REB  "the storm clouds"
NKJV  "flashing clouds"
TEV  "rain clouds"
JPSOA  "storms"

The Hebrew word (BDB 304) is found twice in Job in contexts implying lightning (Job 28:26; 38:15). The thrust of the passage is that YHWH controls the weather and, thereby, food production and fertility (cf. Deut. 11:14-15), not Ba'al.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE WATERS

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This chapter continues the same themes as chapter. 9. The time element is still ambiguous.

  2. Zechariah 10:4 and 11-12 are Messianic. Notice the capitalizations of NASB. The Aramaic Targums also assert these verses as Messianic. However, others see
    1. Zech. 10:4 as referring to Judah
    2. Zech. 10:11-12 as referring to YHWH
      SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIAH
      SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIANIC ERA
    3. The theme of this chapter is the covenant people's dependence on YHWH, not Ba'al. This is the focus of Zech. 10:1. Zechariah 10:2 shows the falsehood that Israel was depending on (cf. Hosea 11:3). The chapter concludes with an emphasis on His people's victorious return in YHWH's name, not a fertility idol's name.
      SPECIAL TOPIC; FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

  3. Notice the numbers of times the FIRST PERSON SINGULAR PRONOUN is used in chapters 9 and 10. YHWH chooses to act Himself to accomplish His redempticve plans. These remind me of Ezek. 36:22-36, which describes the New Covenant based on YHWH's actions, not human performance.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Zechariah 10:2 "teraphim"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:2 "teraphim" This refers to household idols (BDB 1076; NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 339), apparently in humanoid form, used to discern the will of the departed family spirits or the family gods (cf. Gen. 31:19,34; Jdgs. 17:5; 18:14-20; 1 Sam. 15:23; 19:13; 2 Kgs. 23:24; Hosea 3:4). The exact etymology of this term (BDB 1076) is uncertain.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERAPHIM

▣
NASB, Peshitta  "speak iniquity"
NKJV. JPSOA  "speak delusion"
NRSV  "utter nonsense"
TEV  "nonsense"
NJB  "have talked nonsense"
REB  "utter empty promises"
LXX  "utter troubling things"

The VERB (BDB 180, KB 210) is a Piel PERFECT.

The NOUN (BDB 19) basically means "trouble," "sorrow," or "wickedness" (cf. Num. 23:21; Ps. 10:7; 55:11; Isa. 10:1; 55:7; NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 310-312). This Hebrew root has not been found in Semitic cognate languages. Apparently, it is derived from the root for power (i.e., abuse of power).

  1. in worship ‒ 1 Sam. 15:22-23; Isa. 1:13; Hosea 4:15; 5:8; 10:5,8; Amos 5:5; Zech. 10:2
  2. in politics ‒ Isa. 31:2
  3. in law ‒ Isa. 10:1-2; 29:20-21
  4. in war ‒ Ps. 56:7

It is surprising that a list of idolatrous activities is mentioned in the post-exilic period (cf. Mal. 3:5). This whole chapter may be an allusion to Moses' prophecy in Deut. 4:25-31.

▣ "the diviners see lying visions" This is a Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE (BDB 890, KB 1115, "the ones divining") plus a Qal PERFECT VERB (BDB 302, KB 301, "see lies"). Most of these false methods of attempting to find the will of God are mentioned in Deut. 18:9-13, esp. Deut. 18:10 (cf. 2 Kgs. 17:17). Divining is especially mentioned in 1 Sam. 15:23. It either refers to natural (e.g., flight of birds, clouds, sheep livers) or manmade (e.g., casting sticks, tea leaves) means of determining the will of deity (cf. Ezek. 21:21). Here, this term (BDB 890) refers to false prophets (cf. Isa. 3:2; Jer. 27:9; 29:8; Ezek. 13:9,23; 22:38; Micah 3:11).

For a good discussion of "divination" see New International Dictionary of Old Testament Theology and Exegesis, vol. 3, pp. 945-951 or Zondervan's Pictorial Encyclopedia of The Bible, vol. 2, pp. 146-149.

SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVINATION

▣ "And tell false dreams" The VERB (BDB 180, KB 210) is a Piel IMPERFECT. YHWH did often speak through dreams.

  1. Jacob, Gen. 28
  2. Joseph, Gen. 37:39-41
  3. Daniel, Dan. 1:17; 2:4,7

However, sometimes dreams were simply manipulative lies or imaginations of the human subconscious (e.g., Deut. 13:1-5; Jer. 23:32; 27:9-10; 29:8-9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣ "They comfort in vain" The VERB (BDB 636, KB 688) is also a Piel IMPERFECT. The NOUN (BDB 210 I; NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 1003-1004) "vain," or "empty," so common in Ecclesiastes (see full note at Eccl. 1:2), is the same root as "idol" (cf. 2 Kgs. 17:15; Jer. 23:32; 27:9,10). They are nothing, just figments of human superstition and fear, as is this false hope from false prophets!

SPECIAL TOPIC: EMPTY, VAIN, FALSE, NOTHINGNESS

▣ "Therefore the people wander like sheep" The VERB (BDB 652 I, KB 704) is a Qal PERFECT. The term "the people" is in italics, which shows that it is not in the Hebrew text. This verse could refer to the religions leaders, the people, or both. The classic prophetic text about false shepherds and God's flock is in Ezekiel 34, but also is used often by Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 2:8; 10:21; 23:1-2; 50:6).

▣ "They are afflicted, because there is no shepherd" This is a Qal IMPERFECT VERB (BDB 776 III, KB 853) followed by a Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, "shepherding" (BDB 944 I, KB 1258). The concept of shepherd as a title for kings is very common in the ANE (cf. Baldwin, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries, pp. 171-172). The king often stands as a representative of the national god. YHWH is often spoken of as shepherd and His people as sheep (cf. Gen. 49:24; Num. 27:17; Ps. 23:1-2; Isa. 40:11; Ezek. 34:12).

This discussion of a divine shepherd sets the stage for chapters 11-13. Zechariah is unique in his imagery of a wounded shepherd (cf. Zech. 12:10; 13:7), which is theologically parallel to the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53 (the same Hebrew term, "afflicted" (BDB 776 III) is used in Isa. 53:4,7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SUFFERING MESSIAH

entries.title: Zechariah 10:3 "My anger is kindled against the shepherds"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:3 "My anger is kindled against the shepherds" This is another Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE (BDB 944 I, KB 1258) and a Qal PERFECT VERB (BDB 354, KB 351), "is hot." In Ezekiel 34 (esp. Ezek. 34:17) YHWH also condemns His covenant people's civil and religious leaders for their lack of faithfulness to Him.

The term "male goats" may refer to foreign leaders (TEV, cf. Zech. 10:11; Isa. 14:9; Jer. 51:40).

▣ "For the Lord of hosts" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

▣
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta  "has visited"
NRSV, REB  "cares for"
TEV  "will take care of them"
NJB  "comes to visit"
JPSOA  "taken thought"
LXX  "will have concern"

The Hebrew VERB (BDB 823, KB 955, Qal IMPERFECT) means "visited"

  1. for blessing, cf. Zech. 10:3c; Gen. 50:24; Exod. 3:16; 4:31; 13:19
  2. for judgment, cf. Zech. 10:36; 1 Sam. 15:2; Lam. 4:22; Hosea 8:13; 9:9). The best parallel passage is Jer. 23:2. In Zech. 11:16 God allows an evil shepherd to decimate the flock.

▣ "His flock, the house of Judah" This refers to the southern tribes of Judah, Benjamin, Simeon, and most of the tribe of Levi.

The northern remaining tribes were known as

  1. "Israel" (collective name)
  2. Ephraim (largest tribe)
  3. Samaria (the capital city)

This tribal split occurred in 922 B.C. (cf. 1 Kgs. 11:9-13,26-40).

In this chapter Judah is mentioned in Zech. 10:3 and Ephraim in 10:7. This prophet emphasizes their reunification (cf. Zech. 10:6a,b). The post exilic community and the eschatological will be one people (cf. Zech. 10:4d; 6a,b; 8:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

▣ "And will make them like His majestic horse in battle" The VERB (BDB 962 I, KB 1321) is a Qal PERFECT with waw. The term "majestic" (BDB 217 I) is used to describe horses in Job 39:19-25, esp. v. 20. This same word is used in Zech. 6:13 for the majesty of the coming king, but here of His war mount. These are images for YHWH's people being used (cf. Jer. 51:20-33) and honored by His Messiah when He returns to rule and reign.

YHWH is transforming and equipping His people so as to change them from sheep (or devious "he goats") into majestic war stallions (cf. Zech. 9:13). This is an example of the drastic contrasts in prophetic literature (e.g., no war in Zech. 9:10 vs. war in Zech. 9:13; 10:3).

entries.title: Zechariah 10:4 "From them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:4 "From them" The Masoretic Text has "from him" (cf. NKJV, Rotherham, and NAB, also note "He" of Zech. 10:11). There have been several possibilities as to the object of this verse:

  1. it refers to future events, either Maccabean (Selucid) or eschatological
  2. it is a direct reference, which means out of Judah leaders will come (NIV, cf. Zech. 10:3-6; Gen. 49:10; 2 Samuel 7)
  3. the Targums, which are Aramaic translations and interpretations of the Hebrew text, assert that this refers to King Messiah

Notice how YHWH rejects the current leadership who seek information from other places than YHWH (i.e., teraphim, diviners, dreamers) but now He will restore godly, faithful leaders symbolized by

  1. cornerstone (BDB 819)
  2. tent peg (BDB 450)
  3. bow (BDB 905 CONSTRUCT 536)
  4. ruler (BDB 481)

▣ "the cornerstone" This (BDB 819, FEMININE SINGULAR NOUN) refers to the Messiah in Ps. 118:22 and Isa. 28:16 (also FEMININE SINGULAR).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CORNERSTONE

▣ "tent-peg" This Hebrew term (BDB 450) is used of three kinds of pegs.

  1. for tents (cf. Jdgs. 4:21; 5:26; Isa. 33:20; 54:2)
  2. for hanging things on (cf. Isa. 22:22-24; Ezek. 15:3)
  3. for building the tabernacle (cf. Exod. 27:19; 35:18; 38:20,31)

The point of the imagery is

  1. holding ability and thereby permanence (cf. Ezra 9:8; Isa. 22:23)
  2. an ANE sign of the completion of a temple (see IVP Bible Background Commentary [OT], p. 806)

Therefore, the cornerstone was the beginning and the peg the completion.

▣ "the bow of battle" This is a military idiom (cf. Zech. 9:10; Exod. 15:5). The imagery of this verse speak of stability, victory, and unified leadership.

▣ "ruler" This is literally "oppressor." This is the very same Hebrew word (BDB 620) which is used in Zech. 9:8 in a negative sense. However, it seems to be used in a positive sense here (cf. Isa. 60:17) for the administrative or military leaders at the inauguration of the reign of the coming Messiah (cf. Isaiah 9).

entries.title: Zechariah 10:5 "Treading down the enemy in the mire of the streets in battle"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:5 "Treading down the enemy in the mire of the streets in battle" "Treading down" (BDB 100, KB 115, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE; NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 619), possibly "trampling." As YHWH "tramples down" His enemies (i.e., Isa. 14:19,25; 63:6; Ps. 60:12), He empowers His people to trample their enemies (cf. Ps. 44:5; 108:13).

This phrase is a standard idiom of defeat (cf. 2 Sam. 22:43). However, in this context where rain is mentioned (cf. Zech. 10:1) it may refer to mud caused by YHWH's special presence (cf. Jdg. 4-5).

The term "streets" (BDB 299) means "outside streets," which seems to refer to an open market (e.g., Zech. 9:3; 10:5; Isa. 5:25; 10:6; 15:3; 24:11; 51:20,23; Jer. 5:1;7:17,34; 37:21; Ezek. 11:6; 28:23).

▣ "they will fight, for the Lord will be with them" Zechariah 9:1-10 shows that YHWH would do the fighting, but Zech. 9:13-16 and Zech. 10:3-7 seem to say that the Israelites would do the fighting (BDB 535, KB 526 Niphal PERFECT), but with Him in their midst (cf. Jer. 51:20-23).

▣ "the riders on horses will be put to shame" YHWH turns His people into majestic war horses (cf. Zech. 10:3d), but the war horses of the enemies are defeated (BDB 101, KB 116 Hiphil PERFECT with waw, cf. Amos 2:15; Hag. 2:22).

The VERB (i.e., "put to shame," BDB 101, KB 116, Hiphil PERFECT with waw; NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 624) is used often of a defeated army (2 Kgs. 19:26; Isa. 19:9; 37:27; 41:11; Jer. 46:24; 48:20; Ezek. 32:30; Micah 7:16). Remember, in the ANE the defeat and humiliation of a national army meant the humiliation of that nation's deity.

entries.title: Zechariah 10:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:6 Notice the parallelism in the first two lines. YHWH will unify His people (i.e., "Judah" and "Joseph"). Also notice the parallelism of the VERBAL form in which the FIRST PERSON PRONOUN "I" is highlighted in the first three lines. His people are "strengthened" (BDB 149, KB 175 Piel PERFECT with waw) and "saved" (BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil IMPERFECT) because He acts (i.e., Ezek. 36:22-36)! The entire verse reflects His sovereignty, past, present, and future.

Zechariah speaks of YHWH's salvation and deliverance

  1. from the Exile (cf. Zech. 8:7)
  2. from cursing to blessing (Zech. 8:13)
  3. unto an eschatological triumph (cf. Zech. 9:9; 10:6; 12:7)

▣ "Joseph" This is another way of referring to the northern tribes known as Israel, Ephraim (Zech. 10:7), and Samaria.

▣ "I shall bring them back" This word (BDB 996, KB 1427, Hiphil PERFECT with waw; see NET Bible, p. 1674, #5) is a combination of (BDB 998), "bring them back" (NASB, NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB, cf. Zech. 10:10) and "make them dwell" (BDB 442, cf. NASB footnote and Zech. 10:4), which is the translation of the Septuagint. Many rabbis assert that the form is definitely ambiguous so as to emphasize both elements (i.e., repentance and permanent residence in the Promised Land).

▣
NASB, NRSV  "Because I have had compassion on them"
NKJV, Peshitta  "because I have mercy on them"
TEV  "I will have compassion on them"
NJB  "because I have taken pity on them"
REB  "in my compassion for them"
JPSOA  "for I have pardoned them"
LXX  "Because I love them"

This Hebrew VERB (BDB 933, KB 1216, Piel PERFECT) is used often for YHWH's compassion on His people (cf. Exod. 33:19; Deut. 30:3; 2 Kgs. 13:23; Isa. 14:1; 30:18; 49:10,13; 54:8,10; 55:7; 60:10; Jer. 12:15; 30:18; 31:20; 33:26; Hosea 1:6-7; 2:19,23; Micah 7:18-20). This word assured them that YHWH had reestablished the covenant with all of its benefits (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 28). They had experienced the curses!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

▣ "they will be as though I had not rejected them" This verse surely speaks of YHWH's forgiveness and restoration, but it also denotes that He broke the covenant because of His people's sins. It is so difficult to talk about the mercy and forgiveness of YHWH while at the same time reminding humans that the covenant is conditional. He desires fellowship with a holy people. He wants a holy people to reflect His character to a lost world. The old covenant was performance based (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 27-29), but fallen humans were incapable of obedience (cf. Romans 7 and Galatians 3). Therefore, the New Covenant (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-38) is based on

  1. the gracious, unchanging character of YHWH (cf. Mal. 3:6)
  2. the work of the Messiah
  3. the drawing power of the Spirit (cf. John 6:44,65)

The goal is still a righteous people, but the mechanism of that righteousness has changed.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRISTIAN ASSURANCE

▣ "For I am the Lord their God, and I will answer them" The covenant title is made up of the names for Israel's Deity.

  1. YHWH, used in Gen. 2:4 ‒ see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.
  2. Elohim used in Gen. 1:1 ‒ see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

These covenant terms emphasize the restoration of the covenant relationship. Answered prayer (BDB 772 I, KB 851, Qal IMPERFECT) is one of the benefits. The broken covenant is illustrated in Zech. 7:13.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

entries.title: Zechariah 10:7 "Ephraim will be like a mighty man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:7 "Ephraim will be like a mighty man" The northern ten tribes, so devastated by exile, will be reunited with Judah into one family. The term "mighty" (BDB 150) is used of Judah's men in Zech. 10:5.

▣ "their heart will be glad as if from wine" Psalm 104:15 says that wine is a gift from God to gladden the hearts of men. In Zech. 9:15 it described victorious soldiers. Here it is also imagery for joy in military victory provided by YHWH.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

▣ "their children will see it and be glad" This speaks of social stability and peace, as does Zech. 9:17.

▣ "Their hearts will rejoice in the Lord" This same VERB (BDB 162, KB 189, Qal JUSSIVE; NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 955) was used in Zech. 9:9 (Qal IMPERATIVE) at the coming of YHWH. In this verse the root is used of exalting in Him and His acts of deliverance and reestablishment of His people. This verse may be an allusion to Isa. 41:16.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

entries.title: Zechariah 10:8 "I will whistle for them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:8 "I will whistle for them" This (Qal IMPERFECT COHORTATIVE) refers to a characteristic call or sound (i.e., piping) of the shepherd gathering (second VERB, "gather" [BDB 867, KB 1062] is a Piel IMPERFECT used as a COHORTATIVE) his sheep (cf. Jdgs. 5:16). The exact sound is uncertain (BDB 1056, KB 1656), but it is an allusion to YHWH's gathering His scattered people (cf. Isa. 5:26; 7:18,19).

▣ "I have redeemed them" This Hebrew term (BDB 804, KB 911 Qal PERFECT) means to buy back or ransom. Here it is used of YHWH's activity of restoring His people to the Promised Land (cf. Jer. 31:11). Jeremiah 31:10-13 may be the background to Zech. 9:17. Zechariah uses many phrases and terminologies from Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Minor Prophets before his day.

SPECIAL TOPIC: RANSOM/REDEEM

▣ "they will be as numerous as they were before" This context is reminiscent of Jer. 30:18-22. Not only will the remnant return, but YHWH will restore the full number of residents (cf. Ezek. 36:37-38).

One of God's promises to the Patriarchs was that their descendants would be numerous (cf. Gen. 13:16; 15:5; 22:17; 26:4; 28:14; 32:12; Num. 23:10).

entries.title: Zechariah 10:9 "I scatter them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:9 "I scatter them" This context emphasizes the sovereignty of YHWH over history and redemption (cf. Zech. 10:3,6,9,10; Deut. 4:27; 28:64). He acts in blessing and cursing (cf. Lev. 26 and Deut. 27-29) based on His people's obedience to the Mosaic covenant. But even amidst disobedience, He still acts in faithfulness to His own character and purpose (cf. Jer. 31:27-28).

The Hebrew term "scatter" (BDB 281, KB 282, Qal IMPERFECT) can mean "sow" (NKJV). YHWH sowed them because of their idolatry and faithlessness to His covenant (cf. Ezek. 6:9-10), but after judgment they will remember Him and be faithful to Him and teach their children about Him (cf. Deut. 4:9,10; 6:7,20-25; 11:19; 32:46. This was YHWH's plan for taking His message to the world. Often acts of judgment turn into blessings:

  1. the dispersion after the tower of Babel in Genesis 10-11 caused nationalism, which protects humanity from a one-world government
  2. the wilderness wandering period was due to their unbelief, but YHWH turned it into a unique time of His personal care, provision, and presence with His people
  3. Calvary looked so evil and hateful, but God used it for universal redemption
  4. the persecution of the early church resulted in world-wide gospel proclamation (cf. Acts 8:4)

His people did not reach out so He sowed them into the world that He might bring them and others (cf. Zech. 8:20-23) back with them to Himself (see Solomon's prayer in 1 Kings 8, especially vv. 43 and 60)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "they will remember Me" The VERB (BDB 269, KB 269) is a Qal IMPERFECT. This reminds one of Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:46-53). Note the personal element "remember Me," not just the stipulations. Both are part of the covenant relationship.

YHWH's people are to remember what He has done for them (i.e., the Exodus and Conquest) and trust Him in the present difficulties. He acts according to His unchanging, gracious character. Even His judgment is an act of mercy (i.e., Exile).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

▣
NASB, NKJV  "they. . .will live"
NRSV, REB, LXX, Peshitta  "they shall rear"
TEV  "they. . .will survive"
NJB  "they will instruct"
JPSOA  "they shall escape"

The MT has "and they shall live" (BDB 310, KB 309, Qal PERFECT with waw). The UBS Text Project, p. 415, suggests a change of vowels to "and they shall rear," but with a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT

entries.title: Zechariah 10:10 "Egypt. . .Assyria"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:10 "Egypt. . .Assyria" These were the ancient enemies of Israel used to symbolize all of the enemies of YHWH's people.

▣ "the land of Gilead" This was a famous pasture land (cf. Jer. 22:6; 50:19) on the east side of Jordan above the Jabbok River. It was known for its cattle and medicine (cf. Jer. 8:22; 46:11).

▣ "Lebanon" This refers to the realm of Hiram, later called Phoenicia. It was famous for its artisans and lumber (cf. 1 Kgs. 4:33; 5:6,9,14; 7:2; 16:17,21; Isa. 35:2). It was a place of famed beauty and fertility (cf. Sol. 4:8,11,15; 5:15; 7:4). It is included in the Promised Land in Deut. 1:7; 11:24 and Joshua 1:4.

▣ "Until no room can be found for them" This is an idiom of abundance. The Promised Land will be completely filled with YHWH's faithful people.

This multiplication of inhabitants (especially children, cf. Zech. 10:7c) is also mentioned in Isa. 49:14-21 and 54:1-3.

10:11
NASB  "He will pass through the sea of distress"
NKJV, Peshitta  "He shall pass through the sea with affliction"
NRSV  "They shall pass through the sea of distress"
TEV  "When they pass through their sea of trouble"
NJB  "they will cross the sea of Egypt"
REB  "They will pass through the sea of Egypt"
JPSOA  "Ahemmede in force shall pass over the sea"
LXX  "They shall pass through a narrow sea"

As is so common to prophetic and apocalyptic literature, the subject and mood change without notice or textual markers. This is especially true of this context in Zechariah. See Contextual Insights at the beginning of chapter 9.

The problem is trying to find the SUBJECT and OBJECT of Zech. 10:11 and 12. Some assert that

  1. it is the returnees because of Zech. 10:10, "they," LXX
  2. it is the Messiah (MT, "he")
  3. it is YHWH (cf. Zech. 10:12; Isa. 43:2, The Pulpit Commentary, Zechariah, vol. 14, p. 108) and is an allusion to the Exodus (cf. JB and RSV translations)
  4. In my opinion, because Zech. 10:12 implies YHWH and another person ("he"), I believe that these verses are Messianic.

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

▣ "So that all the depths of the Nile will dry up" This is surely a historical allusion to the crossing of the Red Sea (cf. Exod. 15:5) and Jordan Rivers. These were mighty acts of provision. The return from Exile is depicted in the same way (cf. Isa. 44:27). Eschatologically YHWH removes all natural barriers to Himself: rivers, valleys, mountains, as a symbol of a full and free access.

▣ "the pride of Assyria" See note at Zech. 9:6.

entries.title: Zechariah 10:12 "in His name"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:12 "in His name" Zechariah 10:1 begins by saying they were to pray for rain from YHWH, as they had previously been praying to idols. Zechariah 10:12 concludes this thought by asserting that they would walk in YHWH's name and not in the idol's name (cf. Micah 4:5).

Both VERBS

  1. strengthen ‒ BDB 149, KB 175, Piel PERFECT with waw
  2. walk ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Hithpael IMPERFECT

speak of YHWH's power and presence allowing His people to possess, control, and fully enjoy the Promised Land again (i.e., Micah 4:5).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. What is the time element of this chapter? (past, present, near future, or end-time) Why?
  2. Does Zech. 10:2 ever describe the life of the Jewish nation? If so, when?
  3. Why is God called "shepherd" and His people sheep?
  4. List the Messianic references of this chapter.
  5. How and when will Judah and Ephraim be reunited?

entries.title: Zechariah 11:1 "Open your doors"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:1 "Open your doors" This (BDB 834 I, KB 986) Qal IMPERATIVE is imagery for surrender. Zechariah 11:1-3 forms a literary unit. This poem could relate to

  1. chapters 9 and 10, the judgment of YHWH on the surrounding nations
  2. the rest of chapter 11, the judgment of YHWH on His own people

This idiomatic phrase (cf. Isa. 45:1) is a way of personifying the nation of Phoenicia (cf. Zech. 9:3-4). It depicts the military defeat of Phoenicia (Lebanon).

▣ "Lebanon" Lebanon was proverbial for its wealth and power. This poem uses the analogies of certain well-known trees (cedars, cypress, and oak; see UBS' Fauna and Flora of the Bible) and their destruction to describe the judgment of YHWH.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TREES

▣ "a fire may feed on your cedars" The VERB (BDB 37, KB 46, Qal IMPERFECT used as a JUSSIVE) is either an emphasis on YHWH's judgment or an invasion from the north (possibly by YHWH, cf. chapter 9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

entries.title: Zechariah Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
ZECHARIAH 11

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS
